label: Chapter 3
title: The Augustinian Proof
tagline: Eternal truths need an eternal Mind
oneSentence: Universals, propositions, numbers, and possibilities are real, yet they can exist neither in a mindless Platonic “third realm” nor merely in contingent human minds — so they must ultimately exist as an infinite, interlocking system of ideas in one necessarily existing, purely actual, omniscient intellect, which is God.
bigPicture:
Chapter 3 is the odd one out among Feser’s five proofs. The Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Thomistic, and rationalist proofs all start from concrete things — change, composition, the essence/existence distinction, the need for explanation — and argue to their cause. The Augustinian proof starts instead from **abstract objects**: universals like redness and triangularity, propositions like *that snow is white*, numbers, and possible worlds. Feser himself later points out that it is the one argument in the book that is *not a causal argument*, which is why objections like “What caused God?” do not even get a grip on it.

The proof sits on top of one of the oldest debates in philosophy — the problem of universals — and the chapter spends most of its length winning that debate. First Feser argues for **realism** (abstract objects are genuinely real, neither material nor mere human constructs) against **nominalism** (there are only general words) and **conceptualism** (they are products of human minds). Then he sorts through three kinds of realism: **Platonic** (a mind-independent “third realm” of Forms), **Aristotelian** (universals exist in things and, as abstract, only in minds that abstract them), and **Scholastic** (Aristotelian in spirit, but adding that the whole order of eternal truths exists in a divine intellect). Only Scholastic realism survives, and it entails a divine mind.

Stage 2 then shows that this mind is not just a “cosmic mathematician.” The ground of necessary truths must exist necessarily; the eternal truths form one interlocking, infinite system, so one mind must grasp them all; and a necessarily existing intellect must be **purely actual** — which, by the reasoning of Chapter 1, makes it unique, omnipotent, perfectly good, immutable, immaterial, and eternal, and omniscient in the full sense. The idea goes back through Augustine to Neo-Platonism and was defended by Leibniz; Feser gives it a systematic, step-by-step statement.

Why it matters for you: this is the proof that meets the skeptic on the ground of mathematics, logic, and science itself. Anyone who believes that 2 + 2 = 4 was true before humans existed, or that science discovers objective laws, is already halfway into the argument. Your job is to show them where the other half leads.
objectives: Define and give examples of the four kinds of abstract object Feser discusses — universals, propositions, numbers, and possible worlds — and explain why each is not a material thing.
Distinguish realism, nominalism, and conceptualism, and present at least three of Feser’s six direct arguments for realism.
Explain the vicious regress problem and the “words are universals too” problem as refutations of nominalism.
Explain why conceptualism and psychologism undermine themselves, including the argument from communication and the dilemma facing the Kantian version.
State at least three objections to Platonic realism (causal inertness, the Third Man, the animality problem, essences not in things) and explain why the animality problem is decisive.

Contrast Aristotelian and Scholastic realism, and identify the four kinds of case (pure possibles, possibilities with no world, propositions true without minds, necessary truths) that finite minds cannot ground.
Explain why neither human, extraterrestrial, nor angelic minds can be the ultimate ground of necessary truths, and why the “interlocking system” rules out many necessary minds.
Trace how Stage 2 moves from a necessarily existing intellect to pure actuality and thence to the full divine attributes, including unqualified omniscience.
Answer the objections from the concreteness of divine ideas, Leftow’s water example, Grim’s Cantorian argument, and Coffey’s charge of question-begging.

readingGuide.beforeYouRead:
This chapter asks a question you have probably never asked, even though you rely on the answer every day: **what are things like numbers, meanings, and possibilities?** You know that 2 + 2 = 4. You know that “snow is white” means the same thing in English and German. You know Mars *could* have had three moons. But none of these is a physical object you can point to. So what are they, and where are they?

Feser’s answer, drawn from Saint Augustine, is surprising: truths like these are *thoughts*, and because they are eternal and could not have been otherwise, they must be the thoughts of an eternal mind that could not fail to exist — God. Unlike the other proofs in the book, this one is not about causes or the beginning of the universe. It is about the nature of truth itself.

What will you be asked to accept? Mainly things most people already believe: that math and logic are discovered rather than invented; that two people can think the same thought; that something was possible before anyone imagined it. Feser then argues that the popular alternatives — “it’s all just words,” “we made it up,” or “these things float in their own realm” — fall apart when examined.

Some reassurance about the hard parts. The first fifteen pages move through an old debate with a lot of labels (realism, nominalism, conceptualism, Platonic, Aristotelian, Scholastic). Don’t try to memorize them on the first pass; use the map below and the vocabulary list, and focus on the *reasons* each view is accepted or rejected. The section on conceptualism and “psychologism” (pp. 94–97) and the objections at the end (pp. 110–116) are the densest; it is fine to read them twice. Stage 2 borrows one big idea from Chapter 1 — “pure actuality,” meaning having no unfulfilled capacities at all — so glance back at that if it has faded. You don’t need any math beyond simple arithmetic; even the section about Cantor’s theorem is explained below in plain terms.

knowFirst.plain: A general feature many things can share, like redness or roundness. A red ball and a red fire truck both have redness.
Something we can think about and know truths about, but can’t see or touch — such as the number 7 or the meaning of a sentence.
What a sentence means or claims, which can be true or false. The same proposition can be said in many languages.
A complete way things could have been — for example, a world in which Mars has three moons. It is not a real other planet or universe.
Something that couldn’t possibly have been false, like 2 + 2 = 4.
Able to be otherwise or not to exist at all. You are contingent: you might never have been born.
The view that things like numbers and meanings are real, not physical, and not made up by humans.
The view that there are no general features at all — only individual things and the general words we use for them.
The view that general features exist, but only as ideas that human minds construct.
From Chapter 1: being completely “fulfilled,” with no unrealized capacity of any kind. Feser argues only God is like this.

questionsToHold: Where, if anywhere, would 2 + 2 = 4 be true if there were no people and no physical universe?
When you and a stranger think “snow is white,” are you thinking two thoughts or one?
Can anything be “about” something else — represent it — without a mind involved?
Was it possible for humans to exist before there were any humans? What made that true?
Why can’t human minds, which come and go, be the final home of truths that can never change?
Even if some eternal mind holds these truths, what more is needed to show it is God?
For each objection at the end: is the critic disputing a premise, or the definition of a word?

map.section: Informal statement of the argument: Stage 1 (abstract objects)
map.what: The pool-hall example introduces universals; then propositions (“Snow is white” / “Schnee ist weiss”), numbers vs. numerals, and possible worlds. Each is shown to be knowable but not physical.
map.tip: Easy and vivid — read at normal speed. Make sure you can explain why erasing every “2” wouldn’t change arithmetic.

map.section: Stage 1: realism vs. nominalism and conceptualism; direct arguments 1–6
map.what: Feser names the three positions and gives six arguments for realism: one over many, geometry, mathematics, propositions, science, and possible worlds.
map.tip: Slow down on the definitions of the three positions. For each argument, ask: what feature of abstract objects rules out matter and human minds?

map.what: Why “it’s just words” fails: Russell’s resemblance regress, and the point that the word “red” is itself a universal.
map.tip: Read the regress twice, drawing the levels on paper. The type/token idea (one word, many utterances) is the key to argument 8.

map.what: Shared concepts and communication; then Frege’s attack on psychologism, the relativist version, and the Kantian version with its dilemma.
map.tip: The densest stretch of Stage 1. Separate “how did we come to think this way?” from “is what we think valid?” and the self-refutation will become clear.

map.section: Stage 1: Platonic realism and its problems
map.what: Plato’s third realm of Forms, then four objections: causal inertness, the Third Man, the animality problem, and trees reduced to mirror images.
map.tip: The animality argument (pp. 98–99) is the one Feser leans on — reread it until you can state it in two sentences. The Third Man can be skimmed.

map.what: Universals exist in things and, as abstract, only in minds; Oderberg’s squareness quotation; how essences ground possibility and necessity.
map.tip: The key sentence is that nothing is both abstract and mind-independent. Underline it — the rest of the chapter depends on it.

map.section: Stage 1: where Aristotelian realism runs out; Scholastic realism
map.what: Four hard cases (a world possible when none exists, unicorns, truths without minds, necessary truths), then Scholastic realism and the Augustinian thesis of a divine intellect.
map.tip: List the four hard cases in the margin. Notice that Scholastic realism agrees with Aristotle about minds and with Plato about something beyond us.

map.section: Informal statement of the argument: Stage 2
map.what: Why the ground must be a necessarily existing intellect (not human, alien, or angelic); the interlocking system; conceptual omniscience; then pure actuality yielding God’s attributes.
map.tip: Slow down on p. 106, where pure actuality enters — review Chapter 1 if needed. Note the difference between “conceptual” and full omniscience.

map.what: Objectivity, necessity, intentionality, relevance, plenitude, simplicity — and the drawing of Socrates as a carpenter.
map.tip: Make a small table of which condition favors which view. The relevance point about the drawing is the most original idea here.

map.section: A more formal statement of the argument
map.what: The whole argument in 29 numbered steps.
map.tip: Don’t memorize — map it: steps 1–5 (realism), 6–15 (Scholastic realism), 16–29 (one mind, and it is God). Compare with the Argument section of this module.

map.section: Some objections rebutted: are divine ideas “concrete”?
map.what: The objection that ideas in God aren’t abstract, with Feser’s replies and a long footnote on two definitions of “abstract.”
map.tip: Read the footnote carefully: the whole disagreement is about what “abstract” means.

map.section: Some objections rebutted: Leftow on “deity theories”
map.what: The water = H₂O objection, the two-rocks parallel, the impossible “if,” and voluntarism.
map.tip: Keep one idea in view: logical connection is not dependence. The rocks example is your anchor.

map.section: Some objections rebutted: Grim’s Cantorian argument
map.what: Whether Cantor’s theorem rules out a set of all truths, and three replies (Plantinga, Simmons, Wainwright).
map.tip: You don’t need set theory: remember that a set always has more subsets than members, then focus on the three replies.

map.section: Some objections rebutted: Coffey’s charge of begging the question
map.what: A fellow Scholastic’s claim that the argument assumes God, and Feser’s “false choice” reply.
map.tip: Ask of the key premise: could an atheist accept it? Feser’s answer is yes — atheist Platonists do.

afterReading: Without notes, name the four kinds of abstract object and give one example of each.

State the animality argument against Plato in your own words.
List the four hard cases that finite minds can’t ground, and say why an angel wouldn’t do either.
Explain why the eternal truths must be in one mind rather than a committee of minds.

summary.heading: Stage 1 opens: the pool hall and the problem of universals
summary.body:
Feser starts somewhere ordinary: a pool hall. Everything you handle there is a particular, individual thing — this cue, that eight ball, this rack, this table. Yet each is also an *instance* of a general pattern. All the cues leaning on the table share the pattern of being a pool cue; the cue ball and the striped red ball share the pattern of being a billiard ball. And there are wider patterns still: the red balls share **redness** with stop signs, fire engines, and strawberries; all the balls share **roundness** with basketballs, globes, and the moon; the rack shares **triangularity** with pyramids, dinner bells, and dunce caps.

Philosophers call such patterns **universals**. They are called *abstract* because to think of them we set aside — abstract from — whatever individualizes a particular instance. To consider triangularity as such, we ignore that this triangle is wooden and that one stone, that one is green and another orange, that one is printed on a page and another is metal, and attend only to what they share.

Universals exist *at least* as objects of thought: we talk about them meaningfully and know truths about them — whatever is triangular is three-sided, and the angles of a Euclidean triangle add up to two right angles. But no one can see, lift, or bump into triangularity the way one handles a wooden rack. So if triangularity is an object at all, it is an **abstract object**.

Notice the three features Feser has quietly put on the table: universals are *shared by many* things at once, they are grasped by *setting individuality aside*, and they are *knowable without being perceivable*. Everything else in the chapter is an attempt to say what kind of reality could have all three features together.
summary.takeaway: Everyday things are instances of general patterns — universals — which we can know truths about but cannot see or handle, and that makes them abstract objects.
summary.deepDive:
Feser’s opening claim is deliberately modest: universals exist *at least as objects of thought*. He is not assuming realism here. He starts from a datum that nominalists, conceptualists, Platonists, and Aristotelians all accept — we meaningfully talk about triangularity and know truths about it — and only later asks what kind of existence it has. Keep that sequence clear; skipping it makes the argument look as if it assumes its conclusion.

Try a thought experiment. Picture five triangles: a wooden billiard rack, a stone pyramid face, a green paper cutout, an orange road sign, a triangle scratched in sand. Now state something you know: *anything triangular has three sides.* Which of the five is that knowledge about? None in particular — and all of them. It is also about every triangle that will ever be made, and every triangle that could be made but never will be. Your knowledge reaches beyond every particular you have met. That is the mark of a universal.

Notice two nuances. First, Feser adds a qualifier to the angle-sum truth: *at least if it is Euclidean triangles we are talking about*. The truths about universals are precise and relative to exactly what is specified; they are not vague generalizations. Second, universals come in levels of generality. *Being a billiard ball* is shared only by billiard balls; *roundness* is shared by balls, globes, and the moon; *redness* crosses kinds entirely. This layering is an early glimpse of what Stage 2 calls the **interlocking system** (steps 16–17): universals are defined through, and connected to, other universals.

How does this feed the formal argument? It supplies the subject matter of step 1 — the abstract objects whose status is then disputed.

The usual confusion: people hear “abstract” and think *vague*, *unreal*, or *theoretical*. For Feser, “abstract” names the mental act of setting aside individual features. What is grasped that way is not fuzzy at all — triangularity has perfectly exact properties. A second confusion is to think the universal is just the *word* “triangle.” That is precisely the nominalist move Feser will dismantle (step 3).

checks.q: What makes universals “abstract,” in Feser’s explanation?
options: They are vague and imprecise
We consider them by setting aside the individualizing features of particular things
They exist only in the future
They are made of a subtle kind of matter
checks.explanation: “Abstract” refers to abstracting from, or ignoring, what individualizes particular instances. Universals are precise, not vague.

checks.q: Feser’s claim that universals exist “at least as objects of thought” functions as:
options: The conclusion of the entire proof
A proof of Platonic realism
A modest starting point every party accepts, before the question of their mode of existence is raised
A concession to nominalism that universals are unreal
checks.explanation: Everyone agrees we can think about and know truths about triangularity; the dispute is over what kind of existence it has.

summary.plain: Look around a pool hall: every cue and ball is one particular object, but we describe them all with general words like “round,” “red,” and “triangular.” Those general features — philosophers call them universals — are shared by many things at once. You can know facts about “triangle-ness” (it always has three sides), yet you can’t pick it up or see it on its own. That makes it a strange but important kind of thing, and the whole chapter is about what kind.

summary.heading: Three more kinds of abstract object: propositions, numbers, possible worlds
summary.body:
**Propositions** are what sentences express: claims about the world that are true or false, distinct from the sentences used to state them. “John is a bachelor” and “John is an unmarried man” are two sentences with one proposition; so are the English “Snow is white” and the German “Schnee ist weiss.” What a mind entertains when it thinks is ultimately a proposition, not a string of words — which is why Socrates, speaking Greek in fifth-century B.C. Athens, and Barack Obama, speaking English in twenty-first-century Washington, can think exactly the same thing when each thinks that snow is white. A written sentence can be seen and erased; the proposition cannot. Wipe out every token of that sentence in every language and it would still be true that snow is white.

**Numbers** likewise are not the marks we use for them. The numeral “2” is no more the number two than the Roman “II” is — any more than the name “Barack Obama” is the man. Numerals are labels. Erasing every numeral ever written would not make 2 + 2 = 4 false.

**Possible worlds** are ways things could have been: Romney rather than Obama winning in 2012, Mars with three moons or one, a universe whose different physical laws produced no galaxies, unicorns existing alongside horses (or without them). What is possible in this sense is limited by logic, not by physics — physicists themselves consider alternative laws — so there is no possible world where 2 + 2 = 5 or where round squares exist. We can reason about possible worlds, but never visit or perceive them. So here too we have apparent abstract objects.
summary.takeaway: Propositions, numbers, and possible worlds, like universals, are knowable but non-physical: none is identical to the sentence, numeral, or picture we use to represent it.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is the difference between a **representation** and **what is represented**. Feser runs the same test three times: find the physical thing (sentence, numeral, drawing), destroy it, and ask whether the abstract object is harmed. It never is.

A worked example makes the sentence/proposition point vivid. Translate “Snow is white” into ten languages and write each on a card. How many sentences? Ten — different shapes, sounds, word orders. How many propositions? One. If you burn nine cards, you have lost nine sentences and no propositions. If you burn all ten, you still have not made snow stop being white.

There is a subtle nuance worth noticing. When Socrates and Obama each think that snow is white, there are *two acts of thinking*, occurring in two brains, in two eras. But there is *one content* being thought. Many people run these together and conclude that thoughts are private because thinkings are private. Feser’s point is about the content: it is shareable, and that shareability will later be the core of the case against conceptualism (step 4).

Numbers follow the same pattern. A numeral is a *name*, like “Barack Obama.” Destroying every copy of a name does not destroy its bearer. Possible worlds add a twist: they are defined by logic, not physics. Feser stresses that physicists themselves entertain hypotheses about different physical laws, so “possible” here is broader than “physically possible.” Yet it is not unlimited — there is no possible world with round squares.

Where does this feed the argument? These are the abstract objects step 1 is about. Propositions and their logical relations are the backbone of steps 16–17; possible worlds and pure possibles drive step 12 and Welty’s relevance condition.

Common confusions: thinking a possible world is a real parallel universe (it is a way things could have been, not a place); thinking “possible” means “likely”; and thinking a proposition is a belief. A belief is a mental act that can be yours or mine; a proposition is what is believed, and it is the same for both of us.

checks.q: Which pair of sentences expresses a single proposition, according to Feser?
options: “Snow is white” and “Snow is cold”
“Mars has two moons” and “Mars has three moons”
“John is a bachelor” and “John is an unmarried man”
checks.explanation: Different sentences can express one proposition; Feser’s examples include the bachelor pair and “Snow is white” / “Schnee ist weiss.”

checks.q: Which statement about possible worlds matches Feser’s account?
options: They are physically existing parallel universes
They are limited by the actual laws of physics
They are ways things could have been, limited by logic rather than physics
They are simply sentences in books about alternate history
checks.explanation: Physicists consider different laws, so possibility here is not physical possibility; but logic rules out 2 + 2 = 5 and round squares.

checks.q: When Socrates and Obama both think that snow is white, what is shared?
options: One proposition, though the acts of thinking and the languages differ
Only a sentence
The same brain state
Nothing — each has a private thought
checks.explanation: Two acts of thinking, one content. That shared content is the proposition, and its shareability later refutes conceptualism.

summary.plain: Three more things behave the same way. A statement’s meaning (“snow is white”) is the same whether you say it in English or German, and erasing every written copy wouldn’t make it false. Numbers aren’t the ink marks we write for them. And “ways things could have been” — like Mars having three moons — are things we can think about carefully but never visit.

summary.heading: The question: in what sense do abstract objects exist?
summary.body:
Granting that there are, in *some* sense, universals, propositions, numbers, and possible worlds, the real question is what kind of existence they have. Feser canvasses the tempting answers. Perhaps they are merely objects of human thought — conventional entities, constructs of our minds. Perhaps they are just useful fictions. Or perhaps they are material after all, only of an exotic sort — might a universal or a proposition simply be a brain process?

Feser thinks there are compelling reasons to reject all of these and to embrace **realism**: abstract objects are real, cannot be reduced to anything material, and are not sheer constructs of the human mind. Notice that realism has one positive claim (they are real) and two negative ones (not material, not human-made). The two standard rivals each deny one piece. **Nominalism** denies that abstract objects are real at all — there are only particular things and the general words we use. **Conceptualism** grants that they are real but insists that they are wholly constructed by the human mind. A footnote adds that the positions can be mixed: someone might be a realist about numbers and a nominalist about possible worlds, so the arguments must address each kind of abstract object.

It is important what realism, at this stage, does *not* say. It does not yet say *where* or *how* abstract objects exist — in a Platonic realm, in things and minds, or in God. That is a separate question, taken up later.

Feser’s case comes in two waves: six **direct** arguments showing that abstract objects have features (universality, necessity, infinity, independence from matter and from us) that the rivals cannot accommodate, and four **indirect** arguments showing that the rivals undermine themselves.
summary.takeaway: The chapter’s first real question is not whether we can think about abstract objects but what kind of existence they have — and realism answers that they are real, non-material, and not human inventions.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest thing to hold in mind here is that **realism is deliberately noncommittal about location**. People hear “realism about abstract objects” and picture Plato’s heaven of Forms. But in Feser’s usage, Platonists, Aristotelians, and Scholastics are all realists. Step 5 (“some version of realism is true”) is compatible with every one of them; the fight over *where* abstract objects exist begins only at step 6.

A decision tree helps. Question 1: are abstract objects real? If no, you are a **nominalist**. If yes, question 2: are they wholly products of human minds? If yes, you are a **conceptualist**. If no, you are a **realist**. Only then comes question 3: where do real, non-human-made abstract objects exist? That question splits realists into Platonic, Aristotelian, and Scholastic camps. The tree explains why step 1 claims to be exhaustive: every answer to questions 1 and 2 lands in one of three boxes.

What about the option Feser mentions of identifying universals with brain processes? Run it through the tree. Brain processes are particular, located, contingent events in individual heads. If redness *is* such a process, then redness is not one thing shared by many and would not exist without brains — which makes it either not a genuine universal (nominalism) or a product of human minds (conceptualism). The one-over-many argument (step 2) then applies: redness is instantiated where no brain is aware of it.

Feser’s footnote about mixed positions matters for strategy. Because someone might be a realist about mathematics but not about possible worlds, Feser offers arguments tailored to each kind of abstract object — geometry and arithmetic for numbers, a separate argument for propositions, another for possible worlds.

The usual confusion is about the word “conceptualism.” Everyone agrees we *have* concepts. Conceptualism is the stronger claim that universals are *nothing but* human concepts, with no foundation outside our minds. A second confusion is to think that denying abstract objects are human-made means denying they are *mental* in any sense. Keep that door open: the Scholastic will say they are mental — just not merely human.

checks.q: At step 5 (“some version of realism is true”), what has Feser NOT yet claimed?
options: That abstract objects are real
That they are not sheer constructs of the human mind
Where abstract objects exist — a third realm, finite minds, or a divine mind
That nominalism fails
checks.explanation: Realism at step 5 is neutral among Platonic, Aristotelian, and Scholastic versions; step 6 raises the location question.

checks.q: The suggestion that universals are simply brain processes is best classified as:
options: A version of Platonic realism
One of the answers realism rejects, since it makes universals particular, material, and dependent on human minds
Scholastic realism
An instance of the Third Man argument
checks.explanation: Feser lists it among the answers “none of which can be correct.” Brain processes are particular and contingent; universals are shared and instantiated unobserved.

summary.plain: So the big question is: what kind of existence do these things have? One answer says they don’t really exist (there are only words); another says they exist, but only because human minds make them up. Feser defends a third answer, “realism”: they are real, not physical, and not human inventions. At this stage he isn’t yet saying where they exist.

summary.heading: Six direct arguments for realism
summary.body:
1. **One over many.** Triangularity and redness are not any particular triangle or red thing, nor the whole collection of them: all could be destroyed and the universal instantiated again. They are also instantiated when no human is aware of it. So they are neither material things, collections of them, nor mind-dependent.
2. **Geometry.** Geometry discovers objective, necessary truths about perfect lines, angles, and circles (e.g., the angle sum of a Euclidean triangle). We found them, cannot change them, and they held before humans and would hold after us — and whatever happened to the material world, which in any case contains nothing geometrically perfect.
3. **Mathematics in general.** Mathematical truths are necessary and unchanging; the world and human minds are contingent and changing. 2 + 2 = 4 was true before anyone noticed and would survive humanity’s forgetting or the universe’s disappearance. And the number series is **infinite**, while material things and human ideas are finite.
4. **Propositions.** Necessary propositions would be true with no world and no minds — and so would many contingent ones: Caesar’s assassination on the Ides of March would stay true if everything vanished tomorrow. Had nothing material or human ever existed, the proposition *that there is no material world or human mind* would have been true. (Feser cites Plantinga for further problems.)
5. **Science.** Scientific laws and classifications are general, so they refer to universals; science seeks mind-independent facts and is written in mathematics. Accepting science means accepting mind-independent abstract objects.
6. **Possible worlds.** Many possibilities are independent of the actual world and of us: worlds with radically different physics, even ones where humans could not exist; the possibility of a world and minds before either existed; worlds with no matter or human minds at all (say, only angels).
summary.takeaway: Abstract objects have features — universality, necessity, infinity, independence from matter and from us — that neither material things nor human minds can supply.
summary.deepDive:
The six arguments look like a list, but they share one logical form. Each identifies a **feature** of some abstract object and shows that neither the material world nor human minds could have that feature. One over many: a universal survives the destruction of every instance. Geometry: its objects are perfect, and its truths are necessary. Mathematics: its truths are necessary and its objects infinite. Propositions: some are true even in a scenario with no matter and no minds. Science: its laws are general and its facts objective. Possible worlds: many possibilities are prior to, or independent of, anything actual.

Here is a thought experiment that runs several arguments at once — call it the **empty stage**. Imagine that tomorrow every material thing and every human mind ceases to exist. Now ask: is 2 + 2 = 4 still true? Is it still true that Caesar was assassinated on the Ides of March? Is it true that there is no material world and no human mind? Is it possible for a world to exist again? Almost everyone answers yes to all four. But then none of these truths depended on matter or on us.

Notice Feser’s careful qualifications. He does not say *all* possibilities are independent of the actual world — only “much” of what is possible. He says that even many *contingent* propositions (like Caesar’s death) would survive, not just necessary ones. And the argument from mathematics adds something distinctive: the number series is **infinite**, whereas material things and human ideas are finite. That quantitative point will return in Stage 2, where the grounding intellect must grasp an infinite system (step 22).

Most important of all — and the pivot of the whole proof — is what these arguments show independence *from*. They show that abstract objects do not depend on the material world or on *human* (finite) minds. They do **not** show independence from *every* mind. Many readers miss this and think the direct arguments already hand victory to Plato. They do not; they leave open whether some non-human mind is the ground.

These arguments are what step 2 summarizes, and they supply the materials for step 12 later. The usual confusion is to think they already prove God. They do not — a Platonist accepts every one of them. They establish realism; the rest of the chapter asks which realism.

checks.q: What do the six direct arguments show abstract objects to be independent of?
options: The material world and human (finite) minds
Every possible mind, including God’s
Logic
Language only, but not minds
checks.explanation: This is the pivot of the proof: the arguments establish independence from matter and human minds, leaving open dependence on a non-human mind.

checks.q: What distinctive point does the argument from mathematics add?
options: Numbers cause physical events
Numbers are really numerals
Mathematics is a convention
The number series is infinite, while material things and human ideas are finite
checks.explanation: Besides necessity, Feser notes that an infinite series cannot depend on finitely many things or ideas.

checks.q: How would a Platonist respond to the six direct arguments?
options: Reject them all as question-begging
Accept only the argument from science
Take them to prove God’s existence
Accept them, since they establish realism without settling where abstract objects exist
checks.explanation: The direct arguments establish realism. The Platonist agrees; the disagreement comes at steps 6–15.

summary.plain: Feser gives six reasons for realism. Triangle-ness doesn’t disappear if every triangle is destroyed; math truths were true before people existed and can’t be changed by us; there are infinitely many numbers but only finitely many things and thoughts; some truths would hold even if nothing existed; science relies on general laws and math; and many possibilities have nothing to do with us. All of these show independence from the physical world and from human minds — not yet from every mind.

summary.heading: Why nominalism fails
summary.body:
Nominalism says that where we think there are universals, there are really just general *names*: the word “red,” but no such thing as redness. The obvious question is why we apply “red” to exactly these things. The natural answer — because they all have redness — brings universals right back. The nominalist may instead say the things simply *resemble* one another, without saying in what respect. That is implausible on its face (surely they resemble each other *in their redness*), and it runs into two deeper problems.

7. **The vicious regress problem.** As Bertrand Russell pointed out, resemblance is itself a universal. A stop sign resembles a fire truck; grass resembles the Incredible Hulk’s skin; each is a case of one and the same thing, resemblance. If the nominalist says these cases of resemblance are merely called “resemblance” because they resemble one another, we now have a higher-order resemblance — another universal — and the same move just regenerates the problem at each level, forever.
8. **The “words are universals too” problem.** The nominalist says there are no universals, only general words like “red.” But the *word* “red” is a universal: when you, I, and Socrates each say “red,” those are three tokens of one word type. That is the only reason the view ever seemed plausible — one word applying to many things mimics the sense that they have something in common. Deny it, and say our utterances are merely resembling words, and you get absurdity: nobody ever uses the same word twice, even talking to themselves, so communication is impossible — in which case what is the nominalist doing trying to convince us? And the appeal to resemblance reopens the regress.

The general lesson: nominalism is notoriously hard to state without sneaking universals or other abstract objects in through the back door, which makes it self-undermining.
summary.takeaway: Nominalism cannot explain why one word applies to many things without appealing to something shared — resemblance, or the word itself — so it smuggles back the universals it denies.
summary.deepDive:
Russell’s regress is easy to state and easy to misunderstand, so walk it slowly.

*Level 0.* We have red things: a stop sign, a fire truck, a cherry. The nominalist says we call them all “red” because they resemble one another.

*Level 1.* Look at the resemblances themselves: stop sign–fire truck, cherry–ruby, and (for green) grass–Hulk. Each is a case of *resemblance*. Is resemblance a universal — one thing present in many cases? If the nominalist says yes, he has admitted a universal and nominalism is over.

*Level 2.* So he says no: these resemblances are merely called “resemblance” because *they resemble each other*. But now we have a second-order resemblance among resemblances, and the same question arises about it. He faces exactly the same choice again.

The regress is **vicious**, not harmless, because at no level does the nominalist actually explain what he promised to explain. Each level’s account is borrowed from the next, and the debt is never repaid. (Contrast a harmless regress, like the endless series of truths “p is true,” “it is true that p is true,” and so on, where nothing at any level depends on the next for its explanation.)

The “words are universals too” problem is even more direct. The nominalist replaces redness with the *word* “red.” But the word is itself one type with many tokens. Feser’s point is that this is not a minor slip; it is *the* reason nominalism ever sounded plausible. If the nominalist bites the bullet — each utterance is a different word that merely resembles the others — he loses the ability to say anything. Notice a further consequence (a point in the spirit of Feser’s): even logic would collapse, because an argument’s validity depends on the *same* term recurring in premises and conclusion.

How this feeds the argument: this section defends step 3. The usual confusion is to treat nominalism as mere hard-headed common sense (“there are just things and words”). Russell’s point shows the common-sense appeal to resemblance is already a commitment to a universal. A second confusion is to think the debate is “just semantics” — but it is precisely the status of semantics, of shared words and meanings, that is at issue.

checks.q: Why does appealing to resemblance fail to save nominalism?
options: Resemblance is itself a universal, and treating resemblances as merely resembling each other regenerates the problem at every level
Resemblance cannot be observed
Only red things resemble each other
Resemblance is a Platonic Form in a third realm
checks.explanation: This is Russell’s vicious regress: each attempt to avoid the universal resemblance posits a higher-order resemblance.

checks.q: Why is the nominalist’s own word “red” a problem for him?
options: Words are material, so they cannot refer
The word is one type with many tokens — a one-over-many situation — and denying this makes communication impossible
The word “red” is ambiguous
Words exist only in the future
checks.explanation: Your, my, and Socrates’ utterances are tokens of one word; if they are merely resembling words, no one ever uses the same word twice.

checks.q: What makes Russell’s regress vicious rather than harmless?
options: It involves infinitely many objects
It was discovered by Russell
At no level is the promised explanation actually delivered; each level borrows it from the next
It concerns colors
checks.explanation: An infinite series is not bad in itself; it is vicious when each step’s explanation depends on a further step that never completes it.

summary.plain: Some people say there’s no “redness,” only the word “red.” But why use the word for exactly these things? Saying “because they resemble each other” just brings in another shared feature — resemblance — and the problem repeats forever. Worse, the word “red” is itself one thing used by many people; if every use were a different word, nobody could ever communicate.

summary.heading: Why conceptualism fails
summary.body:
Conceptualism tries to split the difference: universals exist, but only in human minds. Feser thinks it faces what are widely regarded as insuperable difficulties.

9. **The objectivity of concepts and knowledge.** When you and I think of redness or triangularity, we entertain *one and the same* concept, referring to one and the same universal — not two private concepts with nothing in common. When we both think of the Pythagorean theorem, we think of one truth, not “your” theorem and “mine.” We share concepts and truths with the long dead and with people not yet born; if humanity died out and new intelligent beings arose, they could grasp the very same ones. So these have a foundation outside the human mind. The same point shows up in **communication**: if the concepts and propositions you express were private constructs, your idea of snow and mine would never be the same, and we could never mean the same thing by anything we said. But we plainly can — indeed we must, even to agree or disagree about conceptualism.
10. **The incoherence of psychologism.** Gottlob Frege fought **psychologism**, the view that the laws of logic and mathematics are just psychological laws describing how human minds happen to work, rather than truths about reality. Add the relativist twist that our minds are shaped by contingent, changing biological, social, historical, and cultural forces, and you get a radical relativism in which logic, math, and science are all culturally conditioned and revisable. That view refutes itself: to explain *how* evolution or culture shaped our minds, you must invoke universals (selection pressures, class interests, genetic mutations, social trends), scientific and mathematical principles, and standards of logic — the very things the view says lack objective validity and did not exist before our minds did.

The less radical, **Kantian** version says our concepts and logic reflect only our own minds’ structure, but *necessarily* so, unchangeable by evolution or culture. This still fails. Its defender must explain how he knows this and how our minds came to be so. If he uses concepts and logic he has just declared cut off from reality, he undermines his case. If he claims to know the necessary, objective structure of our minds, he claims exactly the kind of objective knowledge his theory rules out. Either way he is caught: deny objective validity and he cannot defend his view; affirm it and he contradicts his view in the act of defending it.
summary.takeaway: If concepts were private human constructions, no two people could share a thought or communicate, and every argument for the view would rely on the objective concepts and logic it denies.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is the **self-refutation** at the heart of psychologism, and it becomes clear once you separate two questions: *how did we come to think this way?* (a causal history) and *is what we think valid?* (a question of truth).

Consider a calculator. You can tell a long story about how it was designed, manufactured, and shipped. None of that story settles whether 7 × 8 = 56. The correctness of the output is judged by arithmetic, not by the calculator’s history. Now the relativist offers a history of human minds: evolution and culture shaped us to reason as we do. Suppose that story is true. It still cannot show that our logic lacks validity — and worse, *telling* the story requires the validity it denies. To say “selection pressures produced our logical habits,” you must use universals (selection pressure, mutation, trend), rely on biological and mathematical laws, and draw inferences you expect your listener to accept as valid. If those are merely local habits, so is the argument.

The **Kantian** version is subtler. It concedes that our mental structure is fixed and universal, not culturally variable. Feser’s dilemma: the Kantian claims to *know* something objective — the necessary structure of our minds. Either our concepts and logic give objective knowledge (then his general thesis that they do not reach objective reality is false), or they do not (then he cannot know his thesis). He cannot have it both ways.

Nuances. Feser is not denying that biology or culture influence *how we express* or *come to grasp* truths. His target is the claim that validity *reduces to* those influences. And note what the objectivity argument concludes: concepts and propositions have a foundation *outside the human mind*. It does not say outside *every* mind — which is exactly the opening the Scholastic will use.

This section defends step 4. The usual confusion is to lump conceptualism together with Aristotelian realism, since both put abstract universals in minds. The difference is decisive: the conceptualist says nothing in things answers to our concepts; the Aristotelian says universals exist in things and the mind abstracts them. Another confusion: thinking “we communicate well enough with similar concepts.” But “similar in which respect?” reintroduces a shared concept.

checks.q: Feser’s objection to evolutionary or cultural psychologism is best stated as:
options: Evolution never happened
Culture has no influence on thought
Explaining our logic this way requires appeal to universals, scientific principles, and logical standards that the view says lack objective validity
Kant already disproved it
checks.explanation: The view undermines itself: its own explanation presupposes what it denies.

checks.q: What is the dilemma facing the Kantian conceptualist?
options: If our concepts lack objective validity, he cannot defend his view; if they have it, he has claimed objective knowledge his view rules out
Either God exists or minds evolved
Either universals are in things or in Forms
Either logic is innate or learned
checks.explanation: He must either give up the means of defending his view or contradict it in defending it.

checks.q: What exactly does the argument from the objectivity of concepts conclude?
options: That universals exist in a Platonic third realm
That concepts and propositions have a foundation outside the human mind
That God exists
That concepts are brain states
checks.explanation: It concludes independence from human minds, leaving open whether some non-human mind grounds them.

summary.plain: Others say these things exist, but only as ideas we humans construct. The trouble is that you and I can think the very same thought, which private inventions couldn’t allow — we couldn’t even communicate. And if logic were just a product of evolution or culture, the argument for that claim would itself be just a product of evolution or culture, so it defeats itself.

summary.heading: Three kinds of realism — and the trouble with Plato’s “third realm”
summary.body:
So some realism is true — but which: **Platonic**, **Aristotelian**, or **Scholastic**?

**Platonic realism** (Plato first formulated a version) concludes that abstract objects, depending on neither matter nor human minds, inhabit a *third realm*, neither material nor mental: the Forms, outside space and time, in which particulars “participate” and which they imperfectly “resemble.” On some versions numbers, propositions, and possible worlds are treated the same way. Feser raises several problems:

- **Causal inertness.** A rack arranges balls; a bell makes a sound; an architect’s *concept* of triangularity shapes his pyramid. But triangularity in no thing and no mind seems causally powerless. Then it cannot affect us (so how do we know it?) or particular triangles (so how does it explain their shape?).
- **The Third Man.** A Form seems both universal and an individual thing, so the Form of Man and individual men would need a Super-Form, then a Super-Super-Form, endlessly. Plato raised this himself; its force is disputed.
- **The animality problem** (more telling, Feser thinks). Animality must apply to rational and nonrational animals alike, so it can include neither and in itself is neither. But no individual can be neither rational nor nonrational. So animality cannot be an individual thing in its own right — a Form.
- **Essences outside things.** If treeness is in the Form rather than the tree, a real tree is no more genuinely treelike than a statue or mirror image of one — absurd, especially for the Aristotelian, who regards trees and humans as **substances** with an intrinsic source of their properties and activities.
summary.takeaway: Platonic Forms, existing apart from all minds, could not act, could not be known, could not be both universal and individual, and would drain real things of their natures — so abstract objects cannot exist independently of every mind.
summary.deepDive:
The objection Feser calls “more telling” — the **animality problem** — is the one to master, because it shows not just that Platonism is awkward but that a universal *cannot* exist as a self-standing thing.

A universal is general because it leaves certain things open. *Animality* leaves open whether the animal is rational or not; that is exactly why it can be shared by Socrates and Fido. An individual thing, by contrast, is fully determinate: whatever actually exists as a thing is determinately rational or determinately not. There is no existing animal that is neither. So if animality existed as an individual object in its own right — which is what a Platonic Form would be — it would have to be an existing thing that is neither rational nor nonrational. That is impossible. The generality that makes animality a universal is exactly what prevents it from existing on its own.

A quick exercise helps. Try to imagine “an animal in general” — not a dog, not a human, not a bird. Whatever you picture has some number of legs and some color, and so turns into a particular animal. (Universals can be *conceived* by the intellect, but not *pictured*; and they certainly cannot *exist* as undetermined individuals.)

The **causal inertness** objection has two prongs worth separating. The *epistemic* prong: if a Form affects nothing, how could we know about it? The *explanatory* prong: if a Form affects nothing, how could it explain why a billiard rack is triangular? Even Platonists who deny that knowledge requires causal contact still owe an answer to the second.

Feser’s treatment of the **Third Man** is deliberately modest: Plato raised it himself, and its force has been disputed for millennia. The **mirror-image** objection draws on the Aristotelian notion of **substance**: trees and humans exist in their own right with intrinsic natures, and are not images of something located elsewhere.

This section defends step 10 and so secures step 11. Welty’s intentionality, simplicity, and relevance conditions later add further support.

The usual confusion: when mathematicians call themselves “Platonists,” they usually mean only that numbers are real and discovered. Feser agrees with *that*; it is realism. What he rejects is the claim that abstract objects exist *independently of every mind*. Scholastic realism even keeps one Platonic insight — that there is a reality beyond matter and finite minds.

checks.q: Why does the animality problem show that animality cannot be a Platonic Form?
options: Because animals are material
Because Plato never discussed animals
Because animality must in itself be neither rational nor nonrational, but no existing individual can be neither
Because animality is causally inert
checks.explanation: A universal leaves differences open; an individual is determinate. A Form would be an individual that is somehow undetermined — impossible.

checks.q: What are the two prongs of the causal inertness objection?
options: Forms are too many and too few
Forms cause too much and too little
Forms are material and mental
If Forms affect nothing, we could not know them, and they could not explain why particulars conform to them
checks.explanation: Feser raises both the knowledge problem and the explanation problem.

checks.q: A mathematician says, “I’m a Platonist: numbers are real and we discover truths about them.” How much of this does Feser reject?
options: None of it as stated — that is just realism; he rejects only the claim that abstract objects exist independently of every mind
All of it
Only the claim that we discover mathematical truths
Only the claim that numbers are real
checks.explanation: Feser accepts realism and discovery; his target is the mind-independent third realm.

summary.plain: Plato said these things live in a separate, non-physical, non-mental realm. Feser argues that such things couldn’t do anything, so we couldn’t know about them and they couldn’t explain why real triangles are triangular. Also, “animal in general” is neither human nor non-human, but no real individual thing can be neither — so it can’t exist as a thing by itself. And real trees would become mere copies of the “true” tree elsewhere, which is absurd.

summary.heading: Aristotelian realism: universals in things, abstracted by minds
summary.body:
Aristotelian realism denies the third realm. Outside the mind, animality exists only *in actual animals*, always bound up with either rationality or nonrationality — in Socrates, tied to his rationality and humanness; in Fido, tied to nonrationality and “dogness.” Animality considered *by itself*, stripped of these, exists only in a mind. The senses encounter this man and that dog; the intellect then abstracts away their individualizing and differentiating features and considers animality in isolation, as a universal.

This is **not nominalism**, because universals really exist. It is **not conceptualism**, because universals exist in extramental things themselves (though always tied there to other features); the mind draws them *out of* things rather than freely inventing them. The key thesis is that **abstraction is an intellectual process**, so abstract objects are essentially tied to mind. Humanness, redness, and the rest exist mind-independently, but not *as abstract*; they exist as abstract, but not mind-independently. There is no third way — being abstract and mind-independent at once. Feser quotes David Oderberg to this effect: we do meet squareness all the time — in square things — but we never meet squareness *in the abstract*, because that is something we abstract from square things. Nothing abstract exists without abstraction.

Aristotelians can also explain much of **possibility and necessity** in terms of essences that exist in things. Human nature makes it possible for an ordinary man to hold his breath for ten seconds, impossible for ten hours, and necessary that once dead he cannot be revived by natural means; the mind, abstracting humanness, can deduce these. Two men plus two more make four men, never twenty — a truth grounded in the natures of all things, and the mind abstracting still more general features can derive further mathematics.
summary.takeaway: Universals exist in things concretely and in minds abstractly, but never abstractly and mind-independently at once — nothing abstract exists without abstraction.
summary.deepDive:
The single most important premise in the whole chapter lives here: there is **no third way** for a universal to exist — as both abstract and mind-independent. Everything later depends on it, so it is worth laying out as a grid.

Take humanness. (1) *Concrete and mind-independent*: humanness as it exists in Socrates, bound up with his height, his snub nose, his being in Athens. (2) *Abstract and mind-dependent*: humanness as grasped by an intellect that has set Socrates’ individual features aside. (3) *Abstract and mind-independent*: humanness existing all by itself, in no individual and in no mind. The Aristotelian says box (3) is empty — that was Plato’s box, and the animality problem showed why nothing can occupy it.

Now put that together with realism (step 5). If abstract objects are real, and if they can exist *as abstract* only in an intellect, then wherever there is a real abstract object there is an intellect grasping it. That is the hinge on which the chapter turns from “realism” to “minds.”

Oderberg’s squareness example helps with a natural protest: “But we never *meet* squareness!” Yes we do — in square things. What we never meet is squareness *in the abstract*, because that is not something out there to be met; it is something the intellect produces by abstracting from what it meets. A footnote adds the Scholastic picture of thinking behind this: to think of a thing is for the intellect to take on its form without its matter.

Nuances. Aristotelian realism does real work on **modality**: essences found in things fix what is possible, impossible, and necessary for them — an ordinary man can hold his breath for ten seconds but not ten hours; once dead, he cannot be revived by natural means. Mathematics too can be abstracted from the natures of things (two men plus two men make four). So Feser is not dismissing Aristotle; his objection (next section) is to an Aristotelianism that stops at *finite* minds.

In the formal argument, this section supplies the definition in step 8 and the key thesis that makes step 6’s options exhaustive. The usual confusion: because abstract universals exist only in minds, people conclude the Aristotelian view is “subjective.” But the *content* is drawn from things — the mind finds humanness in Socrates, it does not invent it.

checks.q: Which way of existing does Aristotelian realism say is impossible for a universal?
options: Concretely, in individual things
Abstractly, in an intellect
Abstractly and mind-independently at the same time
Tied to individuating features
checks.explanation: There is no third way; being abstract is the result of an intellect’s abstraction.

checks.q: How can the Aristotelian ground the truth that an ordinary man cannot hold his breath for ten hours?
options: In human nature as it exists in individual men, grasped by the mind’s abstraction of humanness
In a Platonic Form of Breath
In linguistic convention
In divine voluntarism
checks.explanation: Possibilities and necessities for a thing are grounded in its essence, which exists in the thing and is abstracted by the mind.

checks.q: Why is Aristotelian realism not conceptualism?
options: It denies universals are real
It places universals in a third realm
It holds universals exist only in God
It holds universals really exist in extramental things, which the mind abstracts them from rather than inventing them
checks.explanation: The conceptualist says universals are wholly constructed by the mind; the Aristotelian says they exist in things.

summary.plain: Aristotle’s alternative: general features exist inside real things (the “animal-ness” in your dog), and exist as general, abstract ideas only when a mind thinks about them by setting the individual details aside. So nothing is abstract unless some mind is doing the abstracting. This view also explains many facts about what things can and can’t do, based on their natures.

summary.heading: Where Aristotelian realism runs out
summary.body:
But some abstract objects give the Aristotelian — at least one who stops at things and finite minds — serious trouble. Feser lists four kinds of case:

- **Possibility with no world at all.** It is surely possible that no material world and no human minds had ever existed. Yet in that scenario it would *still* have been possible for a world and minds to come into being. What would ground that possibility? Not the essences of material things — there would be none — and not those essences as abstracted by human minds — there would be none of those either.
- **Pure possibles.** Unicorns, centaurs, and mermaids never exist, yet they are possible, and unicornity and the like are (uninstantiated) universals. Their possibility cannot rest on the natures of actual unicorns (there have been none) or on human minds that imagine them (they were possible before anyone imagined them).
- **Propositions true regardless of minds.** The proposition that there is no material world or human mind would be true if both vanished tomorrow, and would have been true had neither existed. Caesar’s assassination, and every historical truth, would stay true too.
- **Necessary truths of mathematics and logic**, which would hold whether or not any world or human mind ever existed, and would survive their disappearance. What grounds *that* necessity?

All four share a structure. The Aristotelian has two grounding resources: natures existing in actual things, and those natures as abstracted by minds. Each case describes a truth or possibility that holds in a situation where neither resource is available, or that holds necessarily while the resources exist only contingently.
summary.takeaway: Some possibilities and truths hold even in scenarios with no matter and no finite minds, so actual things and finite minds cannot be their ultimate ground.
summary.deepDive:
Why should a possibility need a *ground* at all? This is the hardest idea in the section, and it is worth being patient with.

When we say “it is possible that a unicorn exists,” we are saying something true. True claims are true in virtue of something — something in reality answers to them. For actual kinds, the Aristotelian has a good answer: the possibilities for a man are fixed by human nature, which exists in actual men. But for the four cases, both of the Aristotelian’s resources fail.

Try the **empty-stage test**. Imagine a scenario in which there has never been any matter and never any finite mind. Is it, in that scenario, possible for a world to come into being? Feser says surely yes. Now look for the Aristotelian ground: the essences of material things? None exist. Human minds abstracting those essences? None exist. The possibility is left with nothing to rest on — unless there is something beyond matter and finite minds.

Pure possibles make the same point in the actual world. Unicorns were possible before anyone ever imagined one. So imagination did not *make* them possible; it *discovered* that they are. (We cannot imagine a round square into possibility.) And there are no actual unicorns whose nature could ground it.

Notice what Feser concedes: Aristotelian realism handles a great deal — the possibilities of actual kinds, and much of mathematics abstracted from things. His objection is targeted: these four cases need more. He is also careful that the necessary truths problem is about *necessity*: even if human minds happened always to exist, they *could* fail to, and a necessary truth cannot rest on something that might not be there.

This is the case for step 12, which secures step 13 (Aristotelian realism, so defined, is false). It also anticipates Welty’s necessity and plenitude conditions.

The usual confusion is to reply, “The possibility of unicorns is grounded in the atoms and genetics that could produce one.” But in the empty-stage scenario there are no atoms; possibilities with different physics are not grounded in actual physics; and no finite collection of things grounds a necessary truth. A second confusion is to think humanity as a whole, over all history, could serve — but it is just as contingent as any single human.

checks.q: Which case does Feser use to show that Aristotelian realism limited to finite minds is inadequate?
options: An ordinary man holding his breath for ten seconds
Two men plus two men making four men
Fido being an animal
The possibility that a world could come into being even if no world or human minds had ever existed
checks.explanation: The other three are grounded in actual natures abstracted by human minds; the no-world possibility has neither ground available.

checks.q: Why can’t human imagination ground the possibility of unicorns?
options: Because unicorns were possible before anyone imagined them
Because imagination is material
Because unicorns are impossible
Because only scientists can ground possibilities
checks.explanation: Imagining a unicorn discovers a possibility; it does not create it.

summary.plain: But Aristotle’s view, if it stops with human minds, can’t handle some cases. If nothing had ever existed, it would still have been possible for a world to exist — yet there’d be no things or human minds to ground that. Unicorns are possible though none exist and nobody had to imagine them first. And math and logic would be true with no humans around at all.

summary.heading: Scholastic realism and the Augustinian thesis
summary.body:
This brings Feser to **Scholastic realism**, which he describes as essentially Aristotelian in spirit while giving at least a nod to Platonic realism. With Aristotle, it holds that universals exist only either in the things that instantiate them or in intellects that think them — there is no third realm independent of all intellects. With Plato, it agrees that there must be *some* realm distinct both from the material world and from human and other finite minds. Endorsing the thesis famously associated with Saint Augustine, it holds that universals, propositions, mathematical and logical truths, and necessities and possibilities exist in **an infinite, eternal, divine intellect**.

So on the Scholastic view abstract objects have three homes, but none is a mindless realm. Universals exist concretely in things (humanness in Socrates). They exist abstractly in finite intellects that abstract them (humanness in your mind as you read this). And the whole order of universals, propositions, and possibilities exists in the divine intellect — including those no finite mind ever entertains and those that would hold if no finite mind existed.

The Stage 1 argument is thus an argument by elimination: some realism must be true; Platonic and Aristotelian realism are in various ways inadequate; so Scholastic realism is correct — and since it entails an infinite divine intellect, there really is one. Feser notes that this is the basic thrust of what is sometimes called the **argument from eternal truths**, historically associated with Augustinian philosophy and defended also by thinkers like Leibniz. (His introduction adds that the idea has roots in Neo-Platonic thought.) Stage 2 then makes the reasoning more explicit.
summary.takeaway: Scholastic realism keeps Aristotle’s rule that abstract objects exist only in things or in intellects, but adds Plato’s insight that some must exist beyond finite minds — in an infinite, eternal divine intellect.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest thing to see here is how Scholastic realism can agree with *both* Aristotle and Plato without contradiction. The key is to distinguish two different Platonic claims. Plato held (a) that there is a reality beyond matter and finite minds that grounds eternal truths, and (b) that this reality is a realm of mindless Forms. Aristotle rejected (b) — rightly, given the inertness and animality problems. The Scholastic accepts (a) and rejects (b). The eternal truths are real and beyond us, but they are *thoughts*, and the reality that holds them is an intellect.

Compare three pictures of the number seven. **Plato:** seven exists as a Form in a realm by itself; groups of seven things imitate it. **Aristotle (finite minds only):** seven exists in groups of seven things, and as abstract only in minds that count and abstract. **Augustine and the Scholastics:** seven exists in groups of seven things, in finite minds that abstract it, *and* eternally as an idea in the divine intellect — which is why it would still be true that 3 + 4 = 7 if there were no groups and no finite minds.

A common misreading is “Plato plus God”: God as a craftsman who looks up at independent Forms and copies them. That would leave a third realm standing, with God dependent on it. The Scholastic view is the reverse. The eternal truths are not outside God; they are God’s own understanding — which, given divine simplicity, is God himself.

Nuances. The Stage 1 conclusion rests on elimination, so its strength depends on three things: that the three versions are exhaustive (step 6), that Platonism fails (step 10), and that finite minds are inadequate (step 12). Also note Feser’s care in the introduction: this is an Augustinian proof, not an exegesis of Augustine’s texts.

In the formal argument this section corresponds to steps 9 and 14–15. Notice that God enters at step 15 only as “at least one necessarily existing intellect”; the full identification waits until step 27.

The usual confusion: people think the view makes the truths of math *created* by God, as if God could have made them otherwise. No — they are not creatures at all, and not products of an arbitrary choice; they are the eternal content of God’s intellect.

checks.q: What does Scholastic realism accept from Plato?
options: That universals exist in a mindless third realm
That there must be a reality distinct from the material world and from finite minds
That particular things are mere imitations of Forms
That the Third Man argument is decisive
checks.explanation: It accepts that some reality beyond matter and finite minds is needed, but identifies it as a divine intellect, not a realm of Forms.

checks.q: On Scholastic realism, where does humanness exist?
options: Only in a Platonic Form
Only in human minds
Concretely in human beings, abstractly in finite intellects, and ultimately in the divine intellect
Only in God, not in things
checks.explanation: Scholastic realism is Aristotelian in spirit: it keeps universals in things and finite minds and adds the divine intellect.

checks.q: Why is the Scholastic view not “Plato plus a God who copies the Forms”?
options: Because Scholastics deny that God exists
Because the Forms would still be in a third realm
Because Scholastics hold that God invented the Forms by arbitrary choice
Because the eternal truths are God’s own understanding, not independent objects he consults
checks.explanation: No mindless realm remains; the truths are ideas in the divine intellect.

summary.plain: Feser’s answer is “Scholastic realism,” named for the medieval school tradition: keep Aristotle’s view that these things exist only in things or in minds, but add that there must also be a mind beyond all human minds that holds them — an eternal, infinite, divine mind. This idea goes back to Saint Augustine and was later defended by Leibniz. By ruling out the other options, Feser concludes such a mind exists.

summary.heading: Stage 2: the ground must be a necessarily existing intellect
summary.body:
Stage 2 makes the reasoning explicit. The arguments for realism showed that abstract objects (at least a great many of them) do not depend on the material world: material things are always particular, while triangularity and redness are universal; some propositions — especially logical and mathematical ones — hold whether or not the material world exists; the world is contingent while some truths are necessary; and some possibilities would remain possibilities whether or not the world existed. So they must exist in one of the two other ways: in an intellect (or intellects) or in a Platonic third realm. The third realm faces insuperable problems, so they exist in an intellect or intellects.

But not, ultimately, in **human** intellects, which are contingent: they come to be and pass away; once there were none, and someday there may be none again. Necessary truths, possibilities that would hold even if no human ever existed, universals that could be instantiated without humans, and propositions that would be true without humans cannot depend on us. Exactly the same goes for any **contingent creatures**. Suppose there are extraterrestrials with bodies radically unlike ours: because they too come into being, pass away, and could have failed to exist, the same reasoning applies to them. Suppose there are **angels**, pure intellects that never die: they are still contingent, since even an angel exists only if God creates it.

The underlying principle is simple: whatever depends for its existence on something that might not exist might itself fail to exist or hold. So the only kind of intellect on which abstract objects could ultimately depend is one that exists **with absolute necessity** — one that could not possibly have failed to exist.
summary.takeaway: Because every created mind could fail to exist, only an intellect that exists with absolute necessity can be the ultimate ground of truths that hold necessarily.
summary.deepDive:
The engine of this section is a principle about dependence: **what depends on something contingent can be no more necessary than its ground.** Think of a shadow. A shadow depends on an object blocking light. If the object might not exist, the shadow might not exist either. If you found a shadow that *could not fail* to exist, you would know the thing casting it could not fail to exist.

Apply that to 2 + 2 = 4. Suppose its truth depended on human minds. Then in any situation without human minds, it would not be true. But it is true in every situation — that is what necessity means. So its truth cannot depend on human minds. Run the same test with any mind that could fail to exist, and you get the same result.

Notice how thoroughly Feser closes the side doors. Aliens with radically different bodies: still contingent. Angels, who never pass away: still contingent. This last case teaches a distinction many people miss — between **everlasting** and **necessary**. Something could exist forever and still exist only because something else made it so. Necessity is about whether it *could* have failed to exist, not how long it lasts.

Two nuances. First, Feser’s word is “ultimately.” He is not denying that abstract objects exist in human minds — they do, whenever we think (step 9 says they exist in contingent intellects too). The claim is that finite minds cannot be their *ultimate* ground. Second, the argument’s first move repeats something easy to skip: abstract objects cannot simply be located in the material world, because material things are particular and the world is contingent. That is why the only candidates left are intellects and a third realm, and the third realm has already failed.

In the formal argument this reasoning backs step 12 and leads to step 15. It also sets up step 19, since “exists with absolute necessity” is exactly what will be shown to require pure actuality.

The usual confusion: “Why not the universe itself, or the laws of physics, as the necessary ground?” But the material world is contingent and particular, and its laws could have been otherwise — there are possible worlds with different physics. A second confusion is to hear “necessary intellect” and assume the argument has already reached God; it has not yet shown this intellect is one, omniscient, or omnipotent.

checks.q: Why can’t angels be the ultimate ground of necessary truths, even though they never die?
options: Because they are material
Because they cannot think about mathematics
Because everlasting is not the same as necessary: they exist only if created, so they are contingent
Because they are Platonic Forms
checks.explanation: Necessity concerns whether a thing could have failed to exist, not how long it lasts.

checks.q: Feser says abstract objects cannot ultimately depend on human intellects. Does this mean they do not exist in human minds at all?
options: Yes — they exist only in God
No — they exist in human minds when we think, but human minds are not their ultimate ground
Yes — human minds only contain sentences
No — they exist only in material things
checks.explanation: Step 9 says abstract objects exist in contingent intellects too; the claim is about ultimate dependence.

checks.q: What principle drives the move from necessary truths to a necessarily existing intellect?
options: What depends on something that might not exist might itself fail to exist or hold
Every effect resembles its cause
Simpler explanations are always true
Whatever is thought must be spoken
checks.explanation: A necessary truth cannot depend on a contingent ground, so its ultimate ground must be necessary.

summary.plain: Why must that mind be special? Human minds come and go, so truths that are true no matter what can’t depend on them. The same goes for aliens, and even for angels, who never die but still exist only because they were created. So the ultimate home of these truths has to be a mind that could not possibly fail to exist.

summary.heading: One mind, not a committee: the interlocking system and conceptual omniscience
summary.body:
Could there be several necessary intellects — A holding some possible worlds and truths, B holding others? No, because abstract objects are not independent of one another; they form an **interlocking system**, a point Leibniz emphasized. Suppose (just for illustration) a human being is a rational animal. Then adequately grasping humanness requires grasping animality and rationality, which in turn require grasping the universals that define *them* — so grasping any one universal requires grasping a whole network.

Propositions are built from universals: to grasp that all men are mortal you need humanness and mortality. And every proposition is logically related to every other. *All men are mortal* plus *Socrates is a man* entails *Socrates is mortal*; *all men are mortal* plus *cats are four-legged* does not entail *it is raining in Cleveland*. Any two propositions are either consistent or inconsistent; any can be combined with others into compound propositions whose truth values follow the familiar truth tables. Among these are propositions about necessity, possibility, and mathematics.

These logical relationships would hold whether or not the world or any finite mind existed. So there must be a necessarily existing intellect that grasps **all** the logical relationships among **all** propositions (and so all universals), including modal and mathematical ones — so all the abstract objects exist in that one intellect. And their number is **infinite**: for every number there is a true and a false proposition about whether it is odd or even, and every other proposition is consistent or inconsistent with each.
