Such an intellect is omniscient in an obvious sense — in Robert Adams’s phrase, “a conceptually omniscient being” that eternally understands all essences, possibilities, and necessary truths.
summary.takeaway: Because every universal and proposition is logically tied to every other, whatever grounds any of them must grasp all of them — an infinite system held by one conceptually omniscient mind.
summary.deepDive:
Why can’t the eternal truths be divided among several necessary minds? The answer turns on something subtle: **logical relations are themselves truths that need a home.**

Try a concrete case. Suppose necessary mind A holds the proposition *all men are mortal*, and necessary mind B holds *Socrates is a man*. Now consider a third truth: *those two propositions together entail that Socrates is mortal.* Which mind holds that? It relates A’s proposition to B’s, so it can only be grasped by a mind that grasps both. Now generalize. However you try to divide the propositions among minds, there will be logical relations that cross the boundary — and there always are, because Feser points out that *every* proposition is either consistent or inconsistent with every other, and any two can be combined into compound propositions whose truth values follow the truth tables. So some mind must grasp relations that span the whole field — and a mind that grasps all the relations grasps all the propositions they relate. The committee collapses into one member who knows everything the committee was supposed to share.

The same holds for universals. Feser’s illustration — a human being as a rational animal — is explicitly just an example (“whether it is in fact correct is irrelevant”). The point is structural: grasping any universal adequately requires grasping the universals that define it, and those require others, so no universal can be held in isolation.

The system is also **infinite**. For every number there is a true proposition about whether it is odd or even, and a false one; and each of these is consistent or inconsistent with every other proposition. So the intellect that holds the system grasps infinitely many universals, propositions, and possible worlds.

A key nuance: what is established here is **conceptual** omniscience — knowledge of all essences, possibilities, and necessary truths, in Robert Adams’s phrase. Whether this mind also knows contingent facts, like what happened yesterday, is a further question answered only in steps 24–25.

In the formal argument this section is steps 16–18 and 22–23. Note that uniqueness is secured *twice*: informally by the interlocking system, and formally by pure actuality (steps 19–21).

The usual confusion: people hear “omniscient” and assume the argument has already shown God knows everything about everyone. Not yet — Feser is careful to flag the qualification himself.

checks.q: Why do logical relations among propositions block dividing the eternal truths among several minds?
options: Because propositions are material
Because logical relations are unimportant
Because only humans grasp logic
Because any division leaves relations crossing the boundary, which only a mind grasping both sides could hold
checks.explanation: Every proposition is consistent or inconsistent with every other, so some mind must grasp relations spanning the whole system.

checks.q: How does Feser show the system of abstract objects is infinite?
options: For every number there is a true and a false proposition about whether it is odd or even
Because the universe is infinite
Because God is infinite by definition
Because there are infinitely many languages
checks.explanation: The parity example guarantees infinitely many propositions, each logically related to all others.

checks.q: What kind of omniscience does the interlocking-system argument establish on its own?
options: Knowledge of every contingent fact
Conceptual omniscience: knowledge of all essences, possibilities, and necessary truths
Knowledge of the future only
No kind of omniscience
checks.explanation: Adams’s “conceptual omniscience”; full omniscience needs steps 24–25.

summary.plain: Could there be several such minds splitting the work? No: every truth is connected to every other by logic (one follows from another, or they conflict, or they don’t), so any mind holding some of them must hold the connections to all the rest. And since there are infinitely many truths, this one mind knows all the general truths and possibilities there are.

summary.heading: From a conceptually omniscient intellect to God
summary.body:
A critic might still ask: could there be *more than one* conceptually omniscient intellect? Might such a mind know all necessary and possible truths but not contingent ones, making it omniscient only in a qualified sense? And why think it is omnipotent or perfectly good? Is this really God?

Feser answers all three worries with a single move: **pure actuality**. An intellect that exists with absolute necessity must be purely actual. If its existence presupposed the actualization of some potential, it would be contingent on that actualization, and so would not exist of absolute necessity.

Chapter 1 showed what follows from pure actuality. What is purely actual is **unique**: two things of a kind must differ in something one has and the other lacks, and a purely actual being has no material or temporal features and no privations to differ by. It is **omnipotent**, since it is the source of all the actualizing power anything has. It is **perfectly good**, since badness is a privation — a failure to realize a potential — and it has none. It is **immutable**, since change is the actualization of potential; and therefore **immaterial**, **incorporeal**, and **eternal**.

It must also know **all** truths, contingent ones included — otherwise it would have an unactualized potential to know what it does not know, and would not be purely actual. (A footnote adds a second route: the actual is a subset of the possible, so a mind that knows all possible truths knows the actual ones too.)

So realism about abstract objects leads to one necessarily existing intellect that is omniscient, omnipotent, fully good, immutable, immaterial, incorporeal, and eternal: God. Chapter 6 later confirms that this intellect is one and the same as the Unmoved Mover of Chapter 1 and the necessary beings of the other proofs.
summary.takeaway: A necessarily existing intellect must be purely actual, and pure actuality brings uniqueness, full omniscience, omnipotence, perfect goodness, immutability, immateriality, and eternity with it.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest step to see is the first: why does **necessary existence** require **pure actuality**? Unpack the phrase “its existence presupposes the actualization of some potential.” A human intellect is a good contrast. You exist only because countless potentials were actualized — your parents met, a cell divided, your body’s processes keep running right now. Your existence is *conditional*: it holds only if those actualizations occur. Anything whose existence is conditional in that way exists only contingently. So a being that exists with absolute necessity cannot have its existence hanging on any actualization at all. (Chapter 6 adds the same point from another angle: anything with parts of any kind — including a mixture of act and potency — depends on those parts being combined, and so is contingent.)

Now the second hardest step: from pure actuality to **full omniscience**. Think of a student who has not learned calculus. She has a *potential* to know it — a capacity not yet realized. Ignorance, in general, is an unrealized potential to know. A purely actual being has no unrealized potentials. So there is nothing it does not know, including contingent facts. Feser’s footnote gives a second route: every actual truth is among the possible truths, so a mind that knows all possible truths already knows the actual ones.

Notice the economy of this move. Three separate worries — maybe there are several such minds; maybe it knows only necessary truths; maybe it lacks power and goodness — are all answered by one idea borrowed from Chapter 1. That is why Feser can say the five proofs lead to one God rather than five deities: they converge on pure actuality.

In the formal argument this section covers steps 19–21 and 24–27, with steps 20 and 26 imported from Chapter 1.

The usual confusions. First, “pure actuality” does not mean frozen or static; it means lacking nothing that could be added — the opposite of inertness. Second, “necessary” here means absolutely necessary, not merely everlasting (recall the angels). Third, some worry that knowing contingent facts would make God depend on the world. Feser’s Chapter 6 explains that God knows the world as its cause — like an author who knows his story because he is writing it — not by observing it.

checks.q: Why must a necessarily existing intellect be purely actual?
options: Because it knows mathematics
Because if its existence presupposed the actualization of some potential, it would be contingent on that actualization
Because all intellects are purely actual
Because Welty’s simplicity condition requires it
checks.explanation: Conditional existence is contingent existence; absolute necessity rules out any such condition.

checks.q: How does pure actuality yield knowledge of contingent truths?
options: God observes the world as it happens
Contingent truths are really necessary
Ignorance of any truth would be an unactualized potential to know it, which a purely actual being cannot have
It does not; God knows only necessary truths
checks.explanation: Steps 24–25; the footnote adds that the actual is a subset of the possible.

checks.q: Which single idea answers the worries about multiple minds, limited knowledge, and lack of power or goodness?
options: The interlocking system
Welty’s relevance condition
The Third Man argument
Pure actuality, imported from Chapter 1
checks.explanation: Uniqueness, full omniscience, omnipotence, and goodness all follow from pure actuality.

summary.plain: Finally, a mind that couldn’t fail to exist can’t depend on anything outside itself or have any unfulfilled capacity. From the earlier chapter, such a being must be one, all-powerful, perfectly good, unchanging, non-physical, and timeless. And it must know every truth, including everyday facts, because not knowing something would be an unfulfilled capacity. That is what people mean by God.

summary.heading: Welty’s six conditions for a theory of abstract objects
summary.body:
Feser notes that Greg Welty has defended a closely similar argument under the name **Theistic Conceptual Realism** (essentially Feser’s Scholastic realism; Welty uses “conceptualism” more broadly, to include Aristotelian realist views, and Feser judges their differences merely terminological). Welty lists six conditions an adequate theory must meet:

1. **Objectivity** — abstract objects are real independently of human minds.
2. **Necessity** — they exist necessarily, not contingently.
3. **Intentionality** — they *represent*, as thoughts do: triangularity represents triangles, a proposition represents a state of affairs, a possible world represents a way things might have been.
4. **Relevance** — the theory must help explain why there are the necessary and possible truths there are.
5. **Plenitude** — it must posit enough abstract objects to do all the work they are supposed to do.
6. **Simplicity** — it must not multiply kinds of entity beyond need.

Objectivity requires realism rather than nominalism or conceptualism. Intentionality favors minds over a third realm, since it is easier to see how something could have representational content if it is in an intellect. Simplicity favors two realms (matter and intellects) over three. Necessity and plenitude favor Scholastic over merely Aristotelian realism, since finite minds are contingent and countless universals, propositions, and possibilities have never been entertained by any human. **Relevance** favors it too. Borrowing Welty’s example: a drawing of Socrates hammering nails may represent the possibility of Socrates being a carpenter, but it is silly to think Socrates could not have been a carpenter had the drawing never existed. Why would a third-realm “possible world” be any better as the thing that *makes* it possible? The Scholastic answer: a possible world is an idea in the intellect of an omniscient and omnipotent cause who *could have created* that world in accordance with the idea. God’s intellect, will, and power connect abstract objects to what can actually happen, as a third realm cannot.
summary.takeaway: Judged by objectivity, necessity, intentionality, relevance, plenitude, and simplicity, only the view that abstract objects are ideas in God’s mind passes every test.
summary.deepDive:
Welty’s six conditions work best as a **scoreboard**, because each one separates a different pair of rivals.

- *Objectivity* separates realism from nominalism and conceptualism.
- *Intentionality* and *simplicity* separate mind-based views from Platonism.
- *Necessity* and *plenitude* separate the divine intellect from finite minds.
- *Relevance* separates the divine intellect from Platonism again, in a new way.

Only Scholastic realism (Welty’s Theistic Conceptual Realism) wins every row.

The hardest condition is **relevance**, which is really a question about **truthmakers**: what in reality makes a modal truth like “Socrates could have been a carpenter” true? Welty’s drawing shows that *representing* a possibility is not enough. The drawing depicts Socrates with a hammer, yet nobody thinks his possibly being a carpenter depends on that sketch. A Platonic possible world is in the same position: a representation in a realm that has no connection to Socrates or to anything that could act on him.

Now compare an architect. A random sketch of a house on a napkin makes nothing buildable. But the same plan in the mind of a builder with materials and skill is connected to what can actually be built. The Scholastic says possible worlds are like the builder’s plans: ideas in the intellect of an omnipotent cause, who could make them real. That is why they genuinely ground what is possible. (This is also why the chapter’s final picture of God involves intellect, will, and power together, not intellect alone.)

Nuances. Welty himself focuses only on propositions and possible worlds (Feser’s footnote 14), and his use of “conceptualism” is broader than Feser’s — which is why Feser says their disagreement is merely terminological. Also notice that the intentionality point is independent of the earlier animality argument: even if a Platonist could answer the animality problem, he would still owe an account of how mindless objects are *about* anything.

In the formal argument, Welty’s conditions add support to steps 10 and 12. The usual confusions: mixing up the *simplicity condition* (don’t multiply kinds of entity) with *divine simplicity* (God has no parts), and hearing “intentionality” as “intention” (purpose). Here it means representation — aboutness.

checks.q: Which of Welty’s conditions most directly favors placing abstract objects in minds rather than a third realm because they represent things?
options: Plenitude
Objectivity
Necessity
Intentionality
checks.explanation: Representation is intelligible in an intellect; mindless representation is mysterious.

checks.q: What is the point of the drawing of Socrates hammering nails?
options: A representation alone does not make something possible; an idea in the mind of an omnipotent cause can
Socrates really was a carpenter
Pictures are abstract objects
The simplicity condition favors Platonism
checks.explanation: The relevance condition: third-realm worlds are no better truthmakers than drawings.

checks.q: Which pair of conditions favors Scholastic over merely Aristotelian realism?
options: Intentionality and simplicity
Necessity and plenitude
Objectivity and intentionality
Simplicity and objectivity
checks.explanation: Finite minds are contingent (necessity) and have never entertained most abstract objects (plenitude).

summary.plain: The philosopher Greg Welty offers six tests for any theory of these abstract things: they must be real apart from us, necessary, able to “represent” things the way thoughts do, able to explain what’s possible, plentiful enough, and not needlessly complicated. Only the view that they are ideas in God’s mind passes all six. For example, a drawing of Socrates as a carpenter doesn’t make it possible for him to have been one — but a plan in the mind of someone able to make it happen does.

summary.heading: The formal argument in outline
summary.body:
Feser then condenses the reasoning into twenty-nine steps (restated in full in the Argument section of this module). Because the argument grew out of the long debate over universals, it has taken several twists and turns, but its skeleton is simple: two eliminations followed by a deduction.

**First elimination (steps 1–5).** There are only three accounts of abstract objects — realism, nominalism, conceptualism. Realism has decisive arguments in its favor; nominalism and conceptualism face insuperable objections. So some version of realism is true.

**Second elimination (steps 6–15).** Realism comes in three versions — Platonic, Aristotelian, Scholastic — defined by where abstract objects exist: in a third realm, only in contingent intellects, or also in a necessary intellect (steps 7–9 are definitions). The third-realm claim and the contingent-minds-only claim both face insuperable objections (steps 10 and 12), so Platonic and Aristotelian realism are false (11, 13) and Scholastic realism is true (14): abstract objects exist in at least one necessarily existing intellect (15).

**Deduction (steps 16–29).** Abstract objects form an interlocking system, which must exist as a whole in a necessary intellect (16–18). A necessary intellect is purely actual, and only one thing can be purely actual, so there is exactly one (19–21). It is conceptually omniscient (22–23) and, since ignorance would be unrealized potential, omniscient without qualification (24–25). Pure actuality also brings omnipotence, goodness, immutability, immateriality, incorporeality, and eternity (26), so there is exactly one such intellect with all these attributes (27) — which is what it is for God to exist (28–29).

The premises that carry the weight are 2–4, 10, 12, 16–17, 19–20, 24, and 26; the rest are definitions or inferences.
summary.takeaway: The 29 steps are two eliminations — first of realism’s rivals, then of realism’s non-theistic versions — followed by a deduction of God’s attributes from pure actuality.
summary.deepDive:
A long formal argument can feel like a wall of numbered sentences. The way to master it is to ask: **where would a critic have to push to escape the conclusion?** Think of the argument as a building with six exit doors, each deliberately locked.

- **Door 1: nominalism** — “abstract objects aren’t real.” Locked by step 3 (Russell’s regress; words are universals too).
- **Door 2: conceptualism** — “they’re real but human-made.” Locked by step 4 (shared concepts, communication, the self-refutation of psychologism).
- **Door 3: Platonism** — “they’re real and exist in no mind.” Locked by step 10 (inertness, the Third Man, animality, natures exiled from things).
- **Door 4: finite minds** — “they’re in human or other created minds.” Locked by step 12 (pure possibles, possibility without a world, truths without minds, necessary truths).
- **Door 5: a committee** — “several necessary minds share them.” Locked by steps 16–17 and 19–21 (the interlocking system; the uniqueness of pure actuality).
- **Door 6: “that’s not God”** — “a cosmic mathematician, not the God of theism.” Locked by steps 19, 24, and 26 (pure actuality brings full omniscience and every divine attribute).

A critic who wants to reject the conclusion must pick a door and show the lock fails. That is a far more productive conversation than a vague “I’m not convinced.”

Two nuances. First, steps 1 and 6 claim **exhaustiveness** — only three accounts, only three versions of realism. A critic may propose something new (fictionalism, brute modal facts). The Feserian reply is that each new proposal turns out to be a variant of an existing option: fictionalism denies reality (nominalism), brute mind-independent modal facts are Platonism under another name. Second, steps 7–9 are **definitions**, so the substantive work is done by 10 and 12. People sometimes attack step 8 (“Aristotle believed in a divine mind!”), but in the argument “Aristotelian realism” just names the view that stops at contingent minds.

The usual confusion is to think the proof is a single leap from “2 + 2 = 4” to God. It is a chain of eliminations, each backed by pages of argument. Its strength lies in how many independent considerations close each door.

checks.q: Which steps in the formal argument are essentially definitions rather than substantive premises?
options: Steps 7–9
Steps 2–4
Steps 10 and 12
Steps 19–20
checks.explanation: Steps 7–9 say what each version of realism holds; the substantive objections are in 10 and 12.

checks.q: A critic says, “Abstract objects are just brute necessary facts that exist in no mind.” Which step must he attack?
options: Step 3
Step 10, the objections to a mind-independent third realm
Step 26
Step 28
checks.explanation: Real, necessary, mind-independent abstract objects are Platonism in substance, so the critic must defeat step 10.

checks.q: Where in the formal argument do Chapter 1’s results enter?
options: Steps 1 and 6
Steps 7–9
Steps 16–17
Steps 20 and 26
checks.explanation: Step 20 (uniqueness of pure actuality) and step 26 (the other attributes) are imported from Chapter 1.

terms: Argument by elimination (disjunctive syllogism, modus tollens)
summary.plain: Feser then sets out the reasoning in 29 short steps. First he rules out the views that deny these things are real or say we made them up. Then he rules out Plato’s separate realm and the “only human minds” view. Finally he shows the remaining mind must be one, all-knowing, and have all of God’s traditional attributes.

summary.heading: Objection 1: ideas in God would be concrete, not abstract
summary.body:
Feser notes that the debate over abstract objects is over 2,300 years old and entangled with the metaphysics of modality, philosophy of mathematics, and philosophy of language, so he cannot address everything nominalists, conceptualists, or Platonists might say. He takes up several objections aimed specifically at Scholastic realism.

Some critics (Keith Yandell and William Lane Craig, responding to Welty) say that if universals, propositions, and possible worlds are ideas in God’s mind, they are not really *abstract* objects at all but concrete ones. Following Welty, Feser replies first that there is simply no consensus among contemporary metaphysicians about what abstract objects are, so the objection has no settled, neutral definition to lean on. Second, even if there were such a consensus, the objection would beg the question: for Aristotelian and Scholastic realists, an abstract object just *is* what an intellect produces when it abstracts from particulars. The critic says an abstract object cannot exist in an intellect; the Scholastic says it can exist *only* in an intellect. Merely asserting the first does not refute the second; it assumes it false.

In a footnote Feser diagnoses the clash: contemporary philosophers tend to treat thinking as having a “mental state,” a concrete particular in the brain or in a Cartesian soul, whereas for Aristotelians and Scholastics to think is to take on the form of a thing without its matter. They also draw the abstract/concrete line differently — moderns often as outside versus inside space and time, with each thing simply one or the other; Aristotelians in terms of the intellect’s act of abstraction, so the same humanness or redness can exist concretely in things and abstractly in an intellect.
summary.takeaway: Calling divine ideas “concrete” works only on a contemporary definition of “abstract” that the Scholastic rejects; simply asserting that definition begs the question.
summary.deepDive:
This objection is really a clash between two **definitions of “abstract,”** and it dissolves once you see both side by side.

**Contemporary definition.** An abstract object is non-spatiotemporal and causally inert, and in particular is *not* a mental item. Everything is either abstract or concrete, full stop. Thoughts are concrete: they are mental states, particular events in brains or souls.

**Aristotelian-Scholastic definition.** “Abstract” describes the way a nature exists when an intellect has *abstracted* it — considered it apart from the individual features it has in things. The very same nature can exist in two modes: concretely (humanness in Socrates) and abstractly (humanness in your understanding). On this view, abstract objects are *essentially* tied to intellects.

Work through an example. You think about humanness. The contemporary philosopher sees two things: a concrete mental state in your head, and (maybe) an abstract object out in a Platonic realm that the state is about. The Scholastic sees one nature, humanness, existing in you in the abstract mode — the form received without the matter. On the first picture, locating humanness in a mind turns it into a concrete mental state. On the second, locating it in a mind is precisely what makes it abstract.

Feser’s reply therefore has two prongs. First, the contemporary definition is not a neutral consensus — metaphysicians disagree about what abstract objects are (Welty’s point). Second, using that definition against the Scholastic assumes the very thing in dispute. It is like arguing “your view is false because my view is true.”

A nuance worth adding: even if someone insists on calling divine ideas “concrete,” what has been lost? The divine ideas are universal in content, necessary, eternal, and non-physical — everything the Platonist wanted abstract objects to be, minus the mindless realm. The dispute then looks largely verbal.

This defends the Scholastic reading of steps 9 and 15. The usual confusion: imagining God’s thoughts as a stream of separate mental events like ours. Given divine simplicity, God’s understanding is not a series of particular states at all.

checks.q: What does the objection that divine ideas are “concrete” assume?
options: That God does not exist
That Platonic realism is false
The contemporary definition on which abstract objects are non-mental and everything is either abstract or concrete
That nominalism is true
checks.explanation: The Scholastic defines “abstract” by the intellect’s act of abstraction, so the objection begs the question.

checks.q: On the Aristotelian-Scholastic view, how can humanness be both concrete and abstract?
options: It exists concretely in individual humans and abstractly in an intellect that abstracts it
It cannot; that would be a contradiction
It is concrete in God and abstract in humans
It is abstract in a third realm and concrete in the brain
checks.explanation: The same nature exists in two modes, depending on whether the intellect has abstracted it.

summary.plain: Some critics say that if these things are thoughts in God’s mind, they aren’t “abstract” anymore. Feser replies that philosophers don’t agree on what “abstract” means — and on his definition, something is abstract precisely because a mind has abstracted it. So the objection just assumes a definition he rejects.

summary.heading: Objection 2: Leftow and the water example
summary.body:
Brian Leftow criticizes “deity theories,” which ground possibility and necessity in God’s nature. Scholastic realism is one: since God is simple (noncomposite), his intellect, power, goodness, and nature are really one and the same, so grounding necessities in divine ideas is grounding them in the divine nature. Leftow accepts this for pure logic and mathematics but balks at other necessary truths. Suppose it is necessary that water = H₂O. On a deity theory, that necessity follows from God’s nature, so if God exists, water is necessarily H₂O. But then, Leftow says, if it were *not* necessary that water = H₂O, God would not exist — making God’s existence depend on facts about water, which is counterintuitive.

Feser replies with a parallel. It is necessary that 2 + 2 = 4, so it is necessary that two rocks added to two rocks make four rocks. By Leftow’s pattern, if that rock truth were not necessary, 2 + 2 = 4 would not be necessary — so arithmetic “depends” on rocks. Obviously it does not in any interesting sense: mathematics entails necessary truths about rocks as about everything else, and because they are necessary, mineralogy will never overturn them. Likewise the divine nature entails necessary truths about water, and hydrology will never overturn them. Leftow does not claim that hydrology could falsify God’s existence — but then it is very unclear what the supposedly counterintuitive “dependence” amounts to.

Further, why take seriously the antecedent “if it were not necessary that water = H₂O”? If someone proposed to consider a scenario in which 2 + 2 does not necessarily equal 4, we should object that there is no such scenario to consider. The deity theorist can say the same about water (a point Feser credits to Welty). Leftow, a **voluntarist** who thinks such necessities come from God’s will, might say it would not have been necessary had God willed otherwise — but that simply begs the question against deity theorists, who reject voluntarism.
summary.takeaway: That God’s nature entails necessary truths about water no more makes God depend on water than arithmetic depends on rocks — entailment is not dependence.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is why **contraposition does not reveal dependence**. Contraposition is a logical rule: “if P then Q” is equivalent to “if not-Q then not-P.” Leftow starts from “if God exists, water is necessarily H₂O” and contraposes to “if water is not necessarily H₂O, God does not exist.” Logically impeccable. The mistake is to read the second sentence as saying God’s existence *rests on* water.

A famous illustration from the philosophy of science (not from Feser, but it makes his point vivid) is the flagpole and its shadow. Given the sun’s angle, the height of the pole fixes the length of the shadow — and, by the same geometry, the length of the shadow “fixes” the height of the pole. But the shadow does not *explain* or *ground* the pole; the pole explains the shadow. Logical connections run both ways; explanation and dependence run one way. Feser’s rocks example makes the same point with necessary truths: arithmetic entails truths about rocks, but nobody thinks arithmetic is held up by mineralogy.

The second prong targets Leftow’s “if” clause. Conditionals with **impossible** antecedents are strange: if 2 + 2 did not necessarily equal 4, anything at all might “follow.” Feser (following Welty) says the right response is not to entertain the scenario but to deny there is one. If water’s being H₂O is necessary, “suppose it weren’t” describes nothing.

The third prong is the most revealing. Leftow can make the antecedent seem entertainable only by assuming **voluntarism**: necessities about water come from God’s *will*, so God could have willed otherwise. But the deity theorist grounds them in God’s *nature* and intellect, not in arbitrary choice. Assuming voluntarism to refute a deity theory begs the question.

Nuances: Leftow grants deity theories for logic and mathematics; his worry is about other necessities. And the whole deity theory depends on divine simplicity — without it, “grounded in God’s ideas” and “grounded in God’s nature” would come apart.

This defends the coherence of steps 9 and 15. The usual confusion: thinking “grounded in God’s nature” means God could change the truths. It means the opposite — they are as unchangeable as God is. People also sometimes think a truth learned by experience (water = H₂O) must be contingent; how we learn a truth does not settle whether it is necessary.

checks.q: What does Feser’s two-rocks parallel show about Leftow’s objection?
options: That arithmetic depends on rocks
That water is not H₂O
That a necessary truth can entail truths about something without depending on it in any interesting sense
That God wills the laws of chemistry
checks.explanation: Entailment by contraposition is not dependence; hydrology will never overturn God.

checks.q: Why does Feser say Leftow’s appeal to voluntarism fails?
options: Because voluntarism is scientifically disproven
Because it begs the question against deity theorists, who reject voluntarism
Because Leftow is not a voluntarist
Because voluntarism supports Platonism
checks.explanation: Leftow can make the antecedent seem possible only by assuming God could have willed otherwise — exactly what deity theorists deny.

checks.q: Why does divine simplicity matter to this debate?
options: It means God’s ideas and God’s nature are really the same, so grounding truths in divine ideas grounds them in God’s nature
It shows water is simple
It makes God changeable
It means God has no ideas at all
checks.explanation: Scholastic realism counts as a “deity theory” precisely because, in a simple God, intellect and nature are one.

summary.plain: Another critic, Brian Leftow, says that if God’s nature makes “water is H₂O” necessary, then God’s existence would depend on facts about water. Feser answers that arithmetic makes “two rocks plus two rocks is four rocks” necessary, yet arithmetic doesn’t depend on rocks. Logical connection is not the same as dependence.

summary.heading: Objection 3: Grim’s Cantorian argument against omniscience
summary.body:
Another objection targets the very idea of a conceptually omniscient being. It seems to presuppose a *set of all truths*, and Patrick Grim argues there cannot be one. Suppose S is the set of all true propositions. By Cantor’s theorem, the power set of S (the set of all its subsets) has more members than S — and since (the thought runs) each subset generates a further truth, S cannot contain all truths after all. So there is no set of all truths — and, Grim says, no omniscience.

Feser gives three replies. (1) Following Alvin Plantinga, the argument **proves too much**: the same reasoning shows there is no set of all propositions, true or false, yet we coherently say things about all propositions — that every proposition is true or false and none is both. So why can we not coherently say an omniscient being knows all true ones? (2) Following Keith Simmons, omniscience does not require a *set* of known truths: even if there is no such set, it does not follow that there is any particular proposition God fails to know — and that is all omniscience requires. (3) Following William Wainwright, Grim assumes God’s knowledge consists of many discrete ideas forming a set. But given **divine simplicity**, what we describe as God’s grasp of *all men are mortal*, his grasp of *Socrates is a man*, and so on are, in God, one and the same reality described in different ways.

Notice that none of these replies disputes Cantor’s theorem itself. They dispute only the assumption that omniscience requires the truths to form a completed set.
summary.takeaway: Cantor’s theorem at most shows the truths do not form a set; it does not show any truth is unknown to God — and God’s knowledge is not a set of discrete items anyway.
summary.deepDive:
Start with Cantor’s idea in miniature. Take a set with two members, {a, b}. Its subsets are: the empty set, {a}, {b}, and {a, b} — four subsets from two members. With three members you get eight subsets; with *n* members, 2ⁿ. Cantor proved something remarkable: the same holds for infinite sets. The collection of all subsets of any set is always strictly larger than the set.

Grim applies this to truths. Suppose S is the set of all truths. For each subset of S there is a distinct truth about it (for example, that a given truth does or does not belong to that subset). So there are more truths than S contains — contradiction. Hence no set of all truths. Hence, he says, no omniscience.

Now the replies, slowly.

**Plantinga: it proves too much.** The same reasoning rules out a set of all *propositions*. Yet you can confidently assert, “Every proposition is either true or false.” That sentence talks about all propositions without needing them to form a set. If that is coherent, so is “God knows every true proposition.”

**Simmons: no set is needed.** Omniscience can be stated without sets: *for any proposition p, if p is true, God knows p.* That is a universal claim, like “every human is mortal.” Showing that the truths don’t form a set does nothing to produce a *particular* truth God fails to know.

**Wainwright: simplicity.** Grim pictures God’s mind as a vast filing cabinet, each file a separate idea, the whole forming a set. But divine simplicity denies that God’s knowledge is composed of separate items. What we distinguish, from our side, as many acts of knowing are in God one reality.

A nuance: Feser does not challenge Cantor’s mathematics at all. The fight is over a philosophical assumption smuggled in — that knowing everything means possessing a completed collection.

This defends steps 22–25. The usual confusion is thinking “mathematics has refuted God.” What has actually been shown is a limit on *sets*; logicians routinely talk about “all propositions” or “all sets” without treating them as a set.

checks.q: What does Plantinga’s reply to Grim claim?
options: Cantor’s theorem is false
God knows only finitely many truths
Omniscience requires a set of all truths
Grim’s reasoning would equally rule out a set of all propositions, yet we coherently make claims about all propositions
checks.explanation: If the argument worked, we could not say “every proposition is true or false,” but we can.

checks.q: According to Simmons’s reply, what does omniscience require?
options: A completed set of all truths
That there be no particular true proposition God fails to know
Knowledge of all sets
That Cantor’s theorem be false
checks.explanation: Omniscience is a universal claim about propositions, not about possessing a set.

checks.q: Does Feser dispute Cantor’s theorem?
options: Yes — he argues it fails for infinite sets
Yes — he says it is irrelevant to mathematics
No — he disputes only the assumption that omniscience requires the truths to form a set
No — he accepts Grim’s conclusion
checks.explanation: All three replies leave Cantor’s mathematics intact.

summary.plain: A mathematical objection says there can’t be a complete “collection” of all truths, so nobody could know them all. Feser gives three replies: the same reasoning would stop us from saying anything about “all statements,” which we obviously can; knowing everything doesn’t require a collection, only that no truth is left out; and God’s knowledge isn’t a pile of separate items anyway.

summary.heading: Objection 4: Coffey’s charge that the argument begs the question
summary.body:
The last criticism comes from within Scholasticism. Some Scholastics (Peter Coffey; also the Mercier *Manual*) hold that Scholastic realism is true but is not a basis for *proving* God — it is a doctrine to bring in only after God is established on other grounds. Coffey objects that the Augustinian argument presupposes that the possible is eternally and necessarily possible — that horses and unicorns (unlike round squares) were possible before any world or finite mind existed. How could we know this unless we already knew of a necessary intellect grounding it? He also suggests that the idea of an order of abstract objects independent of our minds is a cognitive illusion of the kind Platonism falls into.

Feser finds this weak. First, even an **atheist** can agree that possibilities are eternal and necessary — he will interpret them in Platonic terms, which is exactly why one need *not* presuppose a divine intellect to accept the premise. Second, Coffey, being a Scholastic realist, cannot say such an order is wholly illusory, since he believes it exists in the divine intellect; only the Platonic interpretation of it could be illusory.

Read charitably, Coffey poses a dilemma: whoever affirms a mind-independent order of abstract objects means either (a) a Platonic third realm — which is false — or (b) ideas in God — which is true but question-begging in a proof. Feser calls this a **false choice**. One can affirm that there is an order of abstract objects existing in *some* way independent of all finite minds while leaving open *what* way. That is precisely the common ground on which Platonists and Scholastics debate which view explains it best. Since the Augustinian can accept this thesis without affirming (a), he assumes nothing false; since he can accept it without affirming (b), he begs no question. So Coffey’s objection fails.
summary.takeaway: The Augustinian argument starts from ground that Platonists and Scholastics share — an order of abstract objects independent of finite minds — so it neither assumes a falsehood nor begs the question.
summary.deepDive:
To see why Coffey’s objection fails, get clear on what **begging the question** is. An argument begs the question when one of its premises can only be accepted by someone who already accepts the conclusion. The test is simple: *could someone who rejects the conclusion reasonably accept the premise?*

Apply the test. The disputed premise is that possibilities are eternal and necessary — that horses and unicorns were possible before any world or finite mind existed. Who accepts that? Theists, yes. But also atheist Platonists, who believe possibilities are eternal features of a mindless abstract realm. Since people who reject God accept the premise, it does not presuppose God. Test passed.

A detective analogy helps. “Someone was in the room at midnight” is a premise that does not name the culprit; the detective then eliminates suspects one by one. The Augustinian’s neutral premise is: *there is an order of abstract objects existing in some way independent of all finite minds.* It does not say how. Plato is one suspect (a third realm); God is another (divine ideas). Plato is then eliminated by separate arguments — inertness, animality, intentionality (step 10). No step assumes the answer in advance.

Notice the charity in Feser’s treatment. Coffey is a fellow Scholastic realist; the dispute is not over whether Scholastic realism is true, but over whether it can serve as the *basis* of a proof. Feser also turns Coffey’s own view against the “illusion” charge: a Scholastic cannot call the order of eternal truths an illusion, because he believes it exists in God. What might be illusory is only the Platonic *interpretation* of that order.

This defends the starting points of the argument — especially the claim, used in steps 2, 5, and 12, that abstract objects do not depend on finite minds.

The usual confusion: thinking that because a premise is congenial to theists, it must beg the question. The correct test is whether non-theists can accept it on independent grounds. Here they visibly do — which is why Platonism is a live option in the first place.

checks.q: What is Feser’s first reply to Coffey?
options: Even an atheist Platonist can accept that possibilities are eternal and necessary, so the premise does not presuppose a divine intellect
Possibilities are not eternal
Coffey is not a Scholastic
Unicorns are impossible
checks.explanation: A premise accepted by those who reject the conclusion does not beg the question.

checks.q: Why does Feser call Coffey’s dilemma a “false choice”?
options: Because Platonism is true
Because Coffey misunderstands unicorns
Because God’s existence is self-evident
Because one can affirm an order of abstract objects independent of finite minds while leaving open whether it is Platonic or divine
checks.explanation: That neutral thesis is the common ground on which Platonists and Scholastics then argue.

terms: Argument by elimination (disjunctive syllogism, modus tollens)
summary.plain: One critic, himself a believer, says the argument cheats by assuming what it wants to prove. Feser replies that even atheists who follow Plato agree that possibilities are eternal, so the starting point doesn’t assume God. The argument starts from shared ground and then argues that a divine mind explains it better than Plato’s realm does.

argument.name: The Augustinian proof (the argument from eternal truths)
argument.overview:
The argument is a chain of eliminations followed by a deduction of attributes.

- **Steps 1–5** settle the ancient problem of universals in favor of **realism**: abstract objects are real, neither material nor mere human constructs, because the only alternatives (nominalism and conceptualism) collapse.
- **Steps 6–15** ask *where* realistically construed abstract objects exist. Three answers are possible — a Platonic third realm, only finite (contingent) minds, or also a necessary mind. The first two fail, so abstract objects exist in at least one **necessarily existing intellect**.
- **Steps 16–18** add that abstract objects are not a heap but an **interlocking system**, so the whole system must exist in a necessary intellect.
- **Steps 19–29** bring in Chapter 1: a necessarily existing intellect is **purely actual**, so there is only one; it is **conceptually omniscient** and then **omniscient without qualification**; and it has all the other attributes of pure actuality — which is just to say that God exists.

Notice that the argument is not causal. It never says “something must have caused 2 + 2 = 4.” It asks what kind of reality necessary, eternal, representational truths could have, and answers: only the reality of thoughts in an eternal, necessary mind.

stages.title: Stage 1a — Realism wins
stages.gist: Of the three accounts of abstract objects, nominalism and conceptualism face insuperable objections while realism has decisive support, so realism is true.

stages.title: Stage 1b — Scholastic realism wins
stages.gist: A Platonic third realm and a realism limited to contingent minds both fail, leaving Scholastic realism: abstract objects exist in at least one necessarily existing intellect.

stages.title: Stage 2a — One system, one mind
stages.gist: Abstract objects form one interlocking system that must exist in a necessary intellect, and since a necessary intellect is purely actual and pure actuality is unique, there is exactly one such intellect.

stages.title: Stage 2b — That mind is God
stages.gist: This intellect is conceptually omniscient, then fully omniscient (else it would have unrealized potential), and has every attribute of pure actuality; such a being is God.

steps.text: Abstract objects — universals, propositions, numbers and other mathematical objects, and possible worlds — admit of just three basic accounts: realism, nominalism, or conceptualism.
steps.why: Either abstract objects are not genuinely real (nominalism), or they are real but wholly the product of human minds (conceptualism), or they are real and neither material nor human-made (realism). The other options Feser mentions — mere conventions, useful fictions, or exotic material things such as brain processes — amount to versions of denying their reality or making them mind-made.
steps.example: Ask “Is redness real?” and there are three basic answers: no, there is only the word “red” (nominalism); yes, but only as a concept in our heads (conceptualism); yes, and it is not our invention (realism).
steps.challenge: There are other options — abstract objects as useful fictions, as brain processes, or as brute facts that fit none of these boxes.
steps.answer: Each alternative lands in one of the three: fictionalism denies their reality, brain-process views make them particular products of human minds, and real, non-human-made “brute” abstract facts are simply a form of realism.

steps.text: Realism is supported by decisive arguments.
steps.why: Feser’s six direct arguments: one over many (a universal survives the destruction of all its instances and is instantiated unobserved); geometry (objective, necessary, discovered truths about perfect figures no material thing has); mathematics (necessary truths about an infinite series, while matter and human ideas are contingent and finite); propositions (many would be true with no world and no minds); science (its laws refer to universals and use mathematics); and possible worlds (many possibilities hold independently of the actual world and of us).
steps.example: That 2 + 2 = 4 was true before any human existed, would survive the disappearance of the universe, and belongs to an infinite series no finite collection of things or ideas could match.
steps.challenge: Mathematical truths only seem necessary and objective because of how our minds are built.
steps.answer: That is psychologism, which Feser argues refutes itself (step 4); and the geometry and mathematics arguments show we discover these truths rather than invent them, and cannot change them.

steps.text: Nominalism faces objections it cannot overcome.
steps.why: Asking why we apply “red” to just these things forces an appeal to redness or to resemblance; resemblance is itself a universal and generates a vicious regress (Russell); and the word “red” is itself a universal, one type with many tokens — deny that, and communication becomes impossible. Nominalism keeps smuggling universals back in.
steps.example: When you, I, and Socrates each say “red,” we utter three tokens of one word type — so even the nominalist’s preferred “general word” is a universal.
steps.challenge: The nominalist can take resemblance as a primitive relation needing no further analysis.
steps.answer: A resemblance relation holding among countless different pairs is itself one thing shared by many — a universal — and if the nominalist denies that, Russell’s regress begins.

steps.text: Conceptualism faces objections it cannot overcome.
steps.why: Different people, across languages and centuries, grasp one and the same concept and one and the same truth, and communication requires this; and psychologism, whether in its relativist or its Kantian form, must use objective concepts and logic to state and defend itself, so it refutes itself.
steps.example: You and I, and people centuries dead, all think one and the same Pythagorean theorem — not private versions of it.
steps.challenge: Our concepts need only be similar enough to allow communication; they need not be literally the same.
steps.answer: “Similar enough in which respect?” reintroduces a shared concept; and the conceptualist’s own arguments must use concepts and logic he expects others to grasp as objectively valid.

steps.text: Therefore, some form of realism is correct.
steps.why: From 1–4: if there are only three options and two are eliminated while the third is positively supported, the third stands.
steps.example: Having shown that nominalism and conceptualism collapse while realism is well supported, only realism remains.

steps.text: Realism comes in three possible versions: Platonic, Aristotelian, and Scholastic.
steps.why: Since abstract objects, as abstract, cannot be material things, they exist either in a “third realm” that is neither material nor mental, or in intellects; and if in intellects, either only in contingent ones or also in a necessary one. These are the three versions.
steps.example: The number 7 could exist (a) as a Form in a realm apart from all minds, (b) only in groups of seven things and in the finite minds that abstract it, or (c) also as an idea in a necessary intellect.
steps.challenge: Why not a fourth option — abstract objects simply exist in the material world?
steps.answer: As abstract, they cannot: material things are always particular, while universals are general, and many truths and possibilities hold whether or not the material world exists.

steps.text: On Platonic realism, abstract objects exist in a “third realm” distinct from the material world and from every intellect.
steps.why: This is what defines the Platonic view: the Forms and similar entities exist outside space, time, and all minds, and particular things participate in them.
steps.example: For the Platonist, triangularity exists as the Form of Triangle, in which every billiard rack and pyramid participates.
steps.challenge: Modern Platonists don’t talk about Forms or participation; they just say abstract objects exist.
steps.answer: The label does not matter: any view on which abstract objects exist apart from both matter and every mind is a third-realm view and inherits its problems.

steps.text: On Aristotelian realism, abstract objects exist only in human minds or in other intellects that exist contingently.
steps.why: Aristotelian realism (without a divine intellect) holds that universals exist concretely in things and exist *as abstract* only when some finite intellect abstracts them — and all such intellects are contingent.
steps.example: On this view humanness exists in Socrates and, as abstract, in the minds of those who think about humanity — and nowhere else.
steps.challenge: Aristotle himself believed in a divine intellect, so it is misleading to call a godless view “Aristotelian.”
steps.answer: In the argument the label names a version of realism that stops at contingent minds; Scholastic realism is Aristotelian in spirit and differs only by adding a necessary intellect, so nothing hangs on Aristotle’s own theology.

steps.text: On Scholastic realism, abstract objects exist in contingent intellects and also in at least one intellect that exists necessarily.
steps.why: Scholastic realism agrees with Aristotle that there is no mindless third realm, and with Plato that there must be a realm beyond matter and finite minds — namely, a divine intellect (the Augustinian thesis).
steps.example: The possibility of unicorns exists as an idea in God’s intellect, even though no unicorn ever exists and before any human imagined one.
steps.challenge: Isn’t this just Platonism with the Forms relocated inside God?
steps.answer: No mindless realm remains: the abstract objects are God’s own understanding, not independent objects he consults, so the problems of inert, self-standing Forms do not arise.

steps.text: The claim that abstract objects exist in a third realm apart from both the material world and any intellect faces insuperable objections.
steps.why: Third-realm objects would be causally inert, so we could not know them and they could not explain why things fit patterns; a Form would be both universal and particular, inviting the Third Man regress; animality as an individual would have to be neither rational nor nonrational, which is impossible; and essences exiled from things would make trees no more treelike than mirror images. (Welty’s intentionality, simplicity, and relevance conditions tell against it too.)
steps.example: A Form of Triangle that affects nothing could neither shape a billiard rack nor inform anyone’s mind about triangles.
steps.challenge: Knowledge of mathematics does not require causal contact, so causal inertness is no objection.
steps.answer: Even granting that, an inert Form could not explain why particular things conform to it, and the animality problem shows that a universal cannot exist as an individual thing at all.

steps.text: Therefore, Platonic realism is false.
steps.why: From 7 and 10: Platonic realism just is the third-realm claim, and that claim fails.
steps.example: Since Platonic realism just is the third-realm claim, the failure of that claim is the failure of Platonic realism.

steps.text: The claim that abstract objects exist only in human minds or other contingent intellects faces insuperable objections.
steps.why: Contingent minds come and go, but necessary truths, pure possibles like unicorns, the possibility of a world when none exists, and propositions true whether or not any mind exists cannot depend on them. Finite minds are too few (plenitude) and too contingent (necessity) to ground them; this holds for humans, extraterrestrials, and even angels, who exist only if God creates them.
steps.example: Before any human existed, it was possible for humans to exist — a possibility that could not have depended on human minds.
steps.challenge: Possibilities are grounded in the powers and potentials of actual physical things, so no mind is needed.
steps.answer: That fails where there are no physical things (the possibility of a world when none exists), for possibilities involving different physics, for pure possibles like unicorns, and for necessary truths, which cannot rest on contingent things.

steps.text: Therefore, Aristotelian realism is false.
steps.why: From 8 and 12: Aristotelian realism (as defined here, without a necessary intellect) just is the contingent-minds-only claim, and that claim fails.
steps.example: Aristotelian realism, as defined in step 8, just is the contingent-minds-only claim, so its failure is Aristotelian realism’s failure.

steps.text: Therefore, Scholastic realism is true.
steps.why: From 5, 6, 11, and 13: realism is true, it has only three versions, and two have been eliminated.
steps.example: Like the one door left unlocked after the other two are shown to be locked: realism is true, it has three versions, and two have been eliminated.
steps.challenge: Perhaps there is an overlooked fourth version of realism.
steps.answer: Step 6’s options are exhaustive: real abstract objects exist either apart from all minds (third realm) or in intellects, and intellects are either all contingent or include a necessary one.

steps.text: Therefore, abstract objects exist not only in contingent intellects but in at least one necessarily existing intellect.
steps.why: From 9 and 14: this is what Scholastic realism says.
steps.example: The truth that 2 + 2 = 4 exists as grasped by a necessarily existing intellect, not merely in human minds that come and go.

steps.text: Universals, propositions, mathematical objects, and possible worlds are logically bound up with one another so as to form a single interlocking system of ideas.
steps.why: Grasping a universal requires grasping those that define it (humanness → animality, rationality → …); propositions are composed of universals; and every proposition stands in logical relations — entailment, consistency or inconsistency, truth-functional combination — to every other. Leibniz stressed this.
steps.example: To grasp “all men are mortal” you must grasp humanness and mortality, and that proposition together with “Socrates is a man” entails “Socrates is mortal.”
steps.challenge: Some propositions have nothing to do with each other — “cats are four-legged” is logically irrelevant to rain in Cleveland.
steps.answer: Even unrelated propositions stand in logical relations: they are consistent or inconsistent, their failure to entail each other is itself a logical fact, and they combine into compound propositions with definite truth values.

steps.text: Whatever shows that some abstract objects exist in a necessary intellect also shows that this whole interlocking system must exist in a necessary intellect.
steps.why: The logical relations tying the system together would hold whether or not any world or finite mind existed — exactly the feature that forced us to a necessary intellect in the first place. And since no part of the system can be adequately grasped apart from the rest, it cannot be divided up among separate minds.
steps.example: That “all men are mortal” and “Socrates is a man” together entail “Socrates is mortal” would hold whether or not any finite mind ever thought any of them.
steps.challenge: Why not a division of labor, with different necessary minds holding different clusters of truths?
steps.answer: Any division leaves logical relations crossing the boundary — every proposition is consistent or inconsistent with every other — so some mind must grasp relations spanning the whole system, and that mind grasps it all.

steps.text: Therefore, the interlocking system of ideas exists in at least one necessarily existing intellect.
steps.why: From 15, 16, and 17.
steps.example: The whole web of universals, propositions, and possibilities, with all their logical connections, exists in a necessary intellect.

steps.text: An intellect that exists necessarily would have to be purely actual.
steps.why: If its existence required some potential to be actualized, it would exist only contingently — dependent on that actualization — and so would not exist of absolute necessity.
steps.example: A human intellect exists only because potentials were actualized — conception, growth, ongoing bodily processes; a necessary intellect cannot depend on anything like that.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t something exist necessarily and still have unrealized potentials?
steps.answer: If its existence presupposed any actualization of potential, it would exist only on that condition and so contingently; as Chapter 6 adds, anything composed of act and potency depends on their combination and so is not necessary.

steps.text: There cannot be more than one purely actual being.
steps.why: Established in Chapter 1: two things of a kind must differ by something one has and the other lacks — a material or temporal feature, or some perfection or privation — and a purely actual being, immaterial, eternal, and lacking all privation, has nothing by which it could differ from another.
steps.example: Trees can differ by the sturdiness of their roots and squirrels by whether they have tails (Chapter 1’s examples), but a purely actual being has no material features and no privations to differ by.
steps.challenge: Two purely actual beings might differ merely numerically, without any differing feature.
steps.answer: Things of the same kind are distinguished only by some individuating factor — matter, time, or a perfection one has and the other lacks — and pure actuality has none of these, so there is nothing to make two of them two.

steps.text: Therefore, there cannot be more than one necessarily existing intellect.
steps.why: From 19 and 20: every necessary intellect is purely actual, and there can be only one purely actual thing. Combined with 18, there is exactly one.
steps.example: The imagined “committee” of necessary minds collapses into a single necessary intellect.

steps.text: An intellect containing this interlocking system of ideas would be conceptually omniscient.
steps.why: The system is infinite (for every number there are truths and falsehoods about its parity, each logically related to every other proposition) and includes all essences, possibilities, and necessary truths. A mind grasping all of it knows every essence, possibility, and necessary truth — Adams’s “conceptual omniscience.”
steps.example: Such a mind grasps, for every number, whether it is odd or even, along with every possible essence — including unicornity — and every necessary truth.
steps.challenge: Grasping infinitely many truths is impossible, since Cantor’s theorem shows there is no set of all truths.
steps.answer: Omniscience requires only that no truth goes unknown, not that truths form a set; the argument proves too much; and God’s knowledge is one simple act, not a collection (Plantinga, Simmons, Wainwright).

steps.text: Therefore, the one necessarily existing intellect is conceptually omniscient.
steps.why: From 18, 21, and 22.
steps.example: The one necessary intellect understands all essences, possibilities, and necessary truths — Adams’s “conceptual omniscience.”

steps.text: If this one necessary intellect did not also know every contingent truth, it would have an unactualized potential and so would not be purely actual.
steps.why: Failing to know some truth means having an unrealized capacity to know it. Feser adds in a footnote that the actual is a subset of the possible, so knowing all possible truths already includes the actual ones.
steps.example: A student who has not learned calculus has an unrealized potential to know it; a mind ignorant of any truth likewise has an unrealized potential.
steps.challenge: Knowing contingent facts would make God depend on the world, or change as the world changes.
steps.answer: Feser’s point is only that ignorance is unactualized potential; since the actual is a subset of the possible, knowing all possibilities already includes the actual — and Chapter 6 explains that God knows the world as its cause, like an author knowing his story, not by observing it.

steps.text: Therefore, it is omniscient in the full sense as well.
steps.why: From 19 and 24: it is purely actual, so it cannot have the potential that ignorance of contingent truths would involve.
steps.example: So the necessary intellect knows not only that 2 + 2 = 4 but also what you ate for breakfast this morning.

steps.text: Whatever is purely actual must also be omnipotent, fully good, immutable, immaterial, incorporeal, and eternal.
steps.why: Established in Chapter 1: pure actuality is the source of all actualizing power (omnipotence), lacks all privation (goodness and perfection), cannot change (immutability), and so lacks the potentiality of matter and time (immateriality, incorporeality, eternity).
steps.example: As the source of all actualizing power, pure actuality is omnipotent; lacking every privation, it is perfectly good; unable to change, it is outside time and matter.
steps.challenge: Why should lacking potential make something good in any sense we care about?
steps.answer: For Feser a thing is good to the degree it realizes its nature without privation — as a good painter has actualized the relevant skills — so what lacks all privation is good in the fullest sense (argued in Chapter 1 and developed in Chapter 6).

steps.text: Therefore, there exists exactly one necessarily existing intellect, and it is purely actual, omniscient, omnipotent, fully good, immutable, immaterial, incorporeal, and eternal.
steps.why: Gathering 18, 19, 21, 23, 25, and 26.
steps.example: There is exactly one necessary intellect, and it is purely actual, omniscient, omnipotent, perfectly good, immutable, immaterial, incorporeal, and eternal.

steps.text: For such a being to exist is precisely what it is for God to exist.
steps.why: These are the defining attributes of God in classical theism.
steps.example: This list of attributes is how Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, Maimonides, and the classical tradition describe God.
steps.challenge: The God people pray to is personal and loving, not an abstract intellect.
steps.answer: An intellect that also has will is personal in the classical sense (Chapter 6 treats God’s will and goodness), and the argument reaches the core attributes believers ascribe to God; further truths about God go beyond what natural theology alone establishes.

steps.text: Therefore, God exists.
steps.why: From 27 and 28.
steps.example: God exists as the one necessary mind in which the eternal truths are thought.

keyTerms.definition: Something that exists at least as an object of thought, that we can know truths about, but that cannot be perceived by the senses or physically interacted with — for Aristotelians and Scholastics, specifically what an intellect grasps by abstracting from particulars.
keyTerms.example: Triangularity, the proposition that snow is white, the number 7, a possible world in which Mars has three moons.
keyTerms.origin: From Latin abstrahere, “to draw away”: what the mind draws away from particulars. The contemporary label is from 20th-century analytic metaphysics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Imaginary object — a unicorn image is imaginary; triangularity is abstract but real and knowable, not made up.

keyTerms.definition: A general pattern, nature, or property that many particular things can share or instantiate.
keyTerms.example: Redness, shared by stop signs, fire engines, and strawberries; roundness, shared by billiard balls and the moon.
keyTerms.origin: Latin universalis, “belonging to the whole”; the ancient “problem of universals” goes back to Plato and Aristotle and was named in the Middle Ages.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Collection or set — a universal is not the group of red things but what each of them shares; the group could vanish and redness recur.

keyTerms.definition: The intellect’s act of setting aside a thing’s individualizing features to consider what it shares with others.
keyTerms.example: Ignoring that one triangle is wooden and green and another is stone and orange to consider triangularity as such.
keyTerms.origin: Latin abstrahere, “to draw away from”; central to Aristotle’s and Aquinas’s account of how the intellect knows.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Imagination — imagining forms a picture of one particular triangle; abstraction grasps triangularity itself, which cannot be pictured.

keyTerms.definition: What a sentence expresses or a thought entertains: a claim that is true or false, distinct from any particular sentence or language.
keyTerms.example: “Snow is white” and “Schnee ist weiss” express one proposition, which Socrates and Obama can both think.
keyTerms.origin: Latin propositio, “a setting forth”; the modern notion owes much to Frege, who called it a “thought” (Gedanke).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Sentence — a sentence is a token in some language; the proposition is the language-independent content it expresses.

keyTerms.definition: A numeral is a written or spoken label; a number is the abstract object the label refers to.
keyTerms.example: “2” and “II” are different numerals for one number; erasing every numeral would not make 2 + 2 = 4 false.
keyTerms.origin: Latin numerus, “number”; numerals are the signs, a distinction stressed by Frege.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Digit — a digit is one kind of numeral (0–9); neither a digit nor any numeral is the number itself.

keyTerms.definition: A complete way things could have been, limited by logic rather than by the actual laws of physics.
keyTerms.example: A world in which Romney won in 2012, or unicorns exist; there is no possible world in which 2 + 2 = 5.
keyTerms.origin: The idea goes back to Leibniz (God surveys infinitely many possible worlds); the term was formalized in 20th-century modal logic (e.g., Kripke).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Parallel universe or multiverse — those would be actual physical regions; a possible world is just a way things could have been.

keyTerms.definition: Things that are possible but never actually exist, whose possibility therefore cannot be grounded in any actual instance.
keyTerms.example: Unicorns, centaurs, and mermaids.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic term (possibilia): things possible in themselves though never actual.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Impossibilities — a unicorn is a pure possible; a round square is impossible and has no possible world at all.

keyTerms.definition: A truth that could not have been false and would hold whatever happened to the material world or to any finite mind.
keyTerms.example: 2 + 2 = 4; the angles of a Euclidean triangle sum to two right angles.
keyTerms.origin: Leibniz’s “truths of reason,” as opposed to contingent “truths of fact.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Certain or well-known truth — necessity is about whether it could have been false, not how sure we are of it.

keyTerms.definition: The view that abstract objects are real, not reducible to anything material, and not mere constructs of the human mind.
keyTerms.example: The realist says triangularity would be real and the Pythagorean theorem true even if humanity had never existed.
keyTerms.origin: From Latin res, “thing”; in medieval debates “realists” held that universals are real things, not mere names.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Realism about perception (the external world is real) — a different debate; one can be a realist about tables and a nominalist about redness.

keyTerms.definition: The view that abstract objects are not real; there are only particular things and general words (names) we apply to them.
keyTerms.example: There is the word “red” but no such thing as redness.
keyTerms.origin: Latin nomen, “name”: universals are mere names. Associated historically with Roscelin and William of Ockham.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conceptualism — nominalism denies universals are real; conceptualism grants they are real but only as human mental constructs.

keyTerms.definition: The nominalist claim that we apply one word to many things simply because they resemble each other, without specifying in what respect.
keyTerms.example: Calling a stop sign and a fire truck “red” just because they resemble each other — which Russell showed smuggles in the universal resemblance.
keyTerms.origin: A version of nominalism defended in modern times; Russell’s regress objection is in The Problems of Philosophy (1912), ch. 9.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Realism about resemblance — once resemblance is admitted as a real shared relation, the nominalist has granted a universal.

keyTerms.definition: A type is one general item (such as a word); tokens are its particular occurrences.
keyTerms.example: Your, my, and Socrates’ utterances of “red” are three tokens of one word type — which is why the nominalist’s words are themselves universals.
keyTerms.origin: Distinction coined by the American philosopher C. S. Peirce.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Universal vs. particular in general — type/token is one instance of that contrast, applied to words and symbols.

keyTerms.definition: The view that abstract objects are real but wholly constructed by the human mind.
keyTerms.example: The claim that triangularity exists only as a concept in human heads.
keyTerms.origin: Latin conceptus, “something conceived”; associated with medieval figures such as Abelard (on some readings) and modern thinkers influenced by Locke and Kant.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Aristotelian realism — both say abstract universals exist in minds, but the Aristotelian also holds universals exist in things and are abstracted from them, not invented.

keyTerms.definition: The view (opposed by Frege) that the laws of logic and mathematics are merely psychological laws describing how human minds happen to operate.
keyTerms.example: “Modus ponens is valid only because our brains are wired to think that way.”
keyTerms.origin: German Psychologismus, a 19th-century term; attacked by Frege and Husserl.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Psychology — the empirical study of mental processes is fine; psychologism is the philosophical claim that logic and math reduce to it.

keyTerms.definition: The view that abstract objects exist in a “third realm” outside space, time, matter, and all minds, as Forms that particular things participate in.
keyTerms.example: Triangles are triangles by participating in the Form of Triangle.
keyTerms.origin: Plato; “Form” translates Greek eidos or idea, “look” or “shape.” Participation translates methexis.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Scholastic realism — both posit a reality beyond matter and finite minds, but for Plato it is a mindless realm of Forms, for the Scholastic a divine intellect.

keyTerms.definition: The objection, first raised by Plato himself, that if a Form is itself an individual thing sharing the feature it explains, a further Form is needed to explain it, and so on endlessly.
keyTerms.example: Individual men and the Form of Man would need a Super-Form of Man, and that a Super-Super-Form.
keyTerms.origin: From Plato’s Parmenides; the name (tritos anthrōpos, “third man”) comes from Aristotle’s discussion of it.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Russell’s resemblance regress — the Third Man targets Platonic Forms; Russell’s regress targets nominalist resemblance.

keyTerms.definition: The apparent inability of third-realm abstract objects to cause or affect anything, since they are neither material nor mental.
keyTerms.example: An architect’s concept of triangularity shapes a pyramid, but triangularity in a mindless third realm could affect nothing — not even our knowledge of it.
keyTerms.origin: A standard feature of abstract objects in contemporary metaphysics; the related worry about knowing them is often called Benacerraf’s problem (1973).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Immutability — God is unchanging but not inert; he is the source of all causal power. Platonic Forms would be powerless.

keyTerms.definition: The view that universals exist really but only in the things that instantiate them (bound up with individuating features) and, as abstract, only in intellects that abstract them.
keyTerms.example: Animality exists in Socrates tied to rationality and in Fido tied to dogness; animality in the abstract exists only in a mind.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle; often called “moderate realism” in the Scholastic tradition.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conceptualism — Aristotelian universals exist in extramental things; conceptualist universals exist only in human minds.

keyTerms.definition: In Aristotelian metaphysics, a thing that exists in its own right and has an intrinsic source of its characteristic properties and activities.
keyTerms.example: A tree is a substance, not a mere image of a Form — which is why Plato’s view seems absurd to the Aristotelian.
keyTerms.origin: Latin substantia, “that which stands under,” translating Greek ousia, “being.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Material stuff — in ordinary speech “substance” means a material; in Aristotelian metaphysics it means a thing existing in its own right, like a tree or a person.

keyTerms.definition: Aristotelian realism plus the Augustinian thesis: abstract objects exist in things and finite intellects, and ultimately in an infinite, eternal, divine intellect.
keyTerms.example: The possibility of unicorns is grounded as an idea in God’s intellect.
keyTerms.origin: Latin scholasticus, “of the schools”: the philosophy of the medieval universities (Aquinas and others), drawing on Augustine for the divine-ideas thesis.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Platonic realism — Scholastic realism denies any mindless third realm; the eternal truths are ideas in God.

keyTerms.definition: The traditional name for the Augustinian style of argument, associated with Augustine and Leibniz, from necessary, eternal truths to a divine mind that thinks them.
keyTerms.example: “2 + 2 = 4 is an eternal truth; eternal truths are thoughts; so there is an eternal thinker.”
keyTerms.origin: Augustine argues from unchanging truth to God in On Free Choice of the Will, book 2; Leibniz calls God’s understanding “the region of the eternal truths.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: The design argument — this argument is not about order or fine-tuning in nature but about the status of necessary truths.

keyTerms.definition: The fact that universals, propositions, and other abstract objects are logically interconnected, so that none can be fully grasped apart from the rest.
keyTerms.example: Grasping humanness requires grasping animality and rationality; any two propositions are either consistent or inconsistent.
keyTerms.origin: Emphasized by Leibniz (as discussed by Robert M. Adams).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The coherence theory of truth — that is a theory of what makes beliefs true; the interlocking system is about the logical relations among abstract objects themselves.

keyTerms.definition: Robert Adams’s term for eternally understanding all essences, possibilities, and necessary truths.
keyTerms.example: The necessary intellect of Stage 2 is first shown to be conceptually omniscient, then omniscient without qualification.
keyTerms.origin: Robert Merrihew Adams, Leibniz: Determinist, Theist, Idealist (1994).
