keyTerms.confuseWith: Unqualified omniscience — conceptual omniscience covers essences, possibilities, and necessary truths; full omniscience adds all contingent truths.

keyTerms.definition: Existing with no unactualized potential whatsoever (from Chapter 1); Feser argues a necessarily existing intellect must be purely actual.
keyTerms.example: An intellect ignorant of some truth would have the potential to know it, and so would not be purely actual.
keyTerms.origin: Latin actus purus; rooted in Aristotle’s energeia (actuality) versus dunamis (potentiality).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inactivity or static being — pure actuality is the opposite of lacking activity: it lacks only unrealized potential.

keyTerms.definition: Leftow’s label for theories that ground possibility and necessity in God’s nature, as Scholastic realism does.
keyTerms.example: On a deity theory, the necessity of 2 + 2 = 4 flows from the divine nature.
keyTerms.origin: Brian Leftow’s label in God and Necessity (2012).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Voluntarism — a deity theory grounds necessity in God’s nature; voluntarism grounds it in God’s free will, so it could have been otherwise.

keyTerms.definition: The view that necessary truths (at least some) hold because God wills them, so they could have been otherwise had God willed differently.
keyTerms.example: Leftow’s view that water = H₂O is necessary by God’s choice — which deity theorists reject.
keyTerms.origin: Latin voluntas, “will.” Descartes held that God freely created the eternal truths; Leftow holds a version for some necessities.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Deity theory in general — the Scholastic is a deity theorist but not a voluntarist: necessary truths flow from God’s intellect and nature, not arbitrary choice.

keyTerms.definition: The doctrine that God has no parts, so his intellect, will, power, goodness, and nature are really identical, and his many “ideas” are one reality described in different ways. God is therefore called “simple” or “noncomposite.”
keyTerms.example: It answers Grim: God’s knowledge is not a set of discrete items.
keyTerms.origin: Latin simplex, “single-fold”; classic statement in Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 3; discussed in Feser’s Chapter 2.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Welty’s simplicity condition — that is a methodological rule against multiplying kinds of entity, not a claim that God lacks parts.

keyTerms.definition: Objectivity, necessity, intentionality, relevance, plenitude, and simplicity — criteria for an adequate theory of abstract objects, which Welty argues Theistic Conceptual Realism best satisfies.
keyTerms.example: Intentionality: a proposition represents a state of affairs, as a thought does — so it naturally lives in a mind.
keyTerms.origin: Greg Welty, “Theistic Conceptual Realism,” in Beyond the Control of God? (ed. Paul Gould, 2014).

keyTerms.definition: Whatever it is in reality that makes a given truth true — here, what makes a modal truth (such as “Socrates could have been a carpenter”) true.
keyTerms.example: A drawing of Socrates hammering nails is not what makes it possible for him to have been a carpenter; a divine idea backed by divine power can be.
keyTerms.origin: A term from contemporary metaphysics (e.g., D. M. Armstrong).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Truth-bearer — a truth-bearer (a proposition) is what is true; a truthmaker is what in reality makes it true.

keyTerms.definition: The power set of a set is the set of all its subsets; Cantor proved it always has more members than the original set. Grim uses this against a set of all truths.
keyTerms.example: Answered by Plantinga (proves too much), Simmons (no particular truth goes unknown), and Wainwright (simplicity).
keyTerms.origin: Georg Cantor (1891); Patrick Grim applied it against omniscience (1988).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Subset — a subset is one collection drawn from a set; the power set is the collection of all such subsets.

keyTerms.definition: An individual concrete thing that exhibits a universal. Particulars are located in space and time and can be counted, destroyed, and replaced.
keyTerms.example: The eight ball on this table is a particular; its roundness is shared with the moon.
keyTerms.origin: Latin particularis, “concerning a part.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Token — a token is a particular occurrence of a type (usually of a word or symbol); “particular” is the broader category.

keyTerms.definition: The relation between a particular and a universal it has: the particular instantiates or exemplifies the universal. An “uninstantiated” universal is one that nothing actually has.
keyTerms.example: A stop sign instantiates redness; a pyramid instantiates triangularity.
keyTerms.origin: Latin instantia, “presence”; exemplum, “sample.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Participation — Plato’s term for how things relate to separately existing Forms; instantiation need not assume a third realm.

keyTerms.definition: The ancient question of whether general natures and properties are real, and if so, what kind of existence they have — in things, in minds, or in a separate realm.
keyTerms.example: Is redness something real that stop signs and strawberries share, or just a word we apply to both?
keyTerms.origin: Debated since Plato and Aristotle; named and intensely discussed in medieval philosophy (Boethius, Abelard, Ockham).

keyTerms.definition: The argument that a single universal is present in many particulars and cannot be identified with any one of them or with their collection, since it would survive their destruction.
keyTerms.example: Destroy every triangle in existence; triangularity could still be instantiated in a new one tomorrow.
keyTerms.origin: A classic Platonic argument form; Feser gives it as the first direct argument for realism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Third Man argument — the one over many supports realism; the Third Man is an objection to the Platonic version of it.

keyTerms.definition: For Plato, a Form is an eternal, unchanging, mind-independent exemplar of a kind or property; particular things are what they are by participating in and imperfectly resembling it.
keyTerms.example: The Form of Human Being, in which Socrates and every other man participate.
keyTerms.origin: Greek eidos or idea (“look,” “shape”); participation translates methexis.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Aristotelian (substantial) form — a principle within a thing that makes it what it is, not a separately existing exemplar.

keyTerms.definition: The Platonist’s domain of abstract objects that is neither physical nor mental, existing outside space, time, and all minds.
keyTerms.example: A mathematical Platonist might say the number 7 exists in a third realm, known but not located anywhere.
keyTerms.origin: Frege used the phrase for the realm of thoughts (propositions), distinct from the physical and the psychological.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The divine intellect — Scholastic realism agrees there is a reality beyond matter and finite minds but insists it is a mind.

keyTerms.definition: What a thing is — the set of features that makes it the kind of thing it is and grounds what is possible, impossible, and necessary for it.
keyTerms.example: Human nature makes it possible to hold one’s breath for ten seconds but impossible for ten hours.
keyTerms.origin: Latin essentia, from esse, “to be”; translating Aristotle’s “what it is to be” (to ti ēn einai).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Existence — essence is what a thing is; existence is the fact that it is (the theme of Chapter 4).

keyTerms.definition: Able to exist or not exist, or to be true or false; dependent on conditions that might not have obtained. The noun is “contingency.”
keyTerms.example: Human minds are contingent: once there were none, and there may be none again.
keyTerms.origin: Latin contingere, “to happen, to touch upon.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Uncertain — a contingent truth can be known with certainty (Caesar was assassinated); it is contingent because it could have been otherwise.

keyTerms.definition: A universal that no actual thing has, though it could be had.
keyTerms.example: Unicornity, centaur-ness, and mermaid-ness.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An impossible property — “round-squareness” cannot be instantiated at all; unicornity merely happens not to be.

keyTerms.definition: The ways in which something can be true: possibly, necessarily, contingently, or impossibly. The metaphysics of modality asks what grounds these facts. The adjective is “modal” (as in “modal truths”).
keyTerms.example: It is possible Mars had three moons, necessary that 2 + 2 = 4, impossible that a square is round.
keyTerms.origin: Latin modus, “manner, mode.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Physical possibility — logical/metaphysical possibility is constrained by logic, not by the actual laws of physics.

keyTerms.definition: Existing in such a way that it is impossible not to exist — not depending on anything else or on any potential being actualized. A being with this feature is “necessarily existing” or a “necessary being.”
keyTerms.example: Stage 2 argues that the intellect grounding necessary truths must exist necessarily, unlike humans or angels.
keyTerms.origin: Developed in Avicenna, Aquinas, and Leibniz; tied in Feser to pure actuality.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Everlasting existence — an angel may never cease to exist, yet it exists contingently because God might not have created it.

keyTerms.definition: The “aboutness” of abstract objects: like thoughts, they represent something beyond themselves.
keyTerms.example: The proposition that all men are mortal represents the state of affairs of all men being mortal.
keyTerms.origin: Latin intendere, “to aim at”; revived as a technical term by Brentano.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Intention in the sense of purpose — intentionality here is representation, not planning to do something.

keyTerms.definition: Two of Welty’s tests: plenitude requires enough abstract objects to do all the work they are posited for; relevance requires that they help explain why there are the necessary and possible truths there are.
keyTerms.example: Relevance: an idea in an omnipotent mind of Socrates as carpenter explains why he could have been one; a drawing does not.
keyTerms.origin: Greg Welty, “Theistic Conceptual Realism” (2014).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Simplicity condition — plenitude asks for enough entities; simplicity forbids more kinds than necessary.

keyTerms.definition: Greg Welty’s name for the view that abstract objects are thoughts in God’s mind — essentially what Feser calls Scholastic realism.
keyTerms.example: Welty argues this view best satisfies all six of his conditions.
keyTerms.origin: Greg Welty (2014).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conceptualism in Feser’s sense — Welty’s “conceptualism” is broader and includes Aristotelian realism; Feser’s conceptualism means human-mind-made universals.

keyTerms.definition: The eternal exemplars of all possible things, truths, and essences as they exist in God’s intellect.
keyTerms.example: The possibility of a world with unicorns exists as a divine idea, whether or not God creates unicorns.
keyTerms.origin: Augustine (drawing on Neo-Platonism), later Aquinas and Leibniz.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Human concepts — our concepts are learned by abstraction and many; God’s ideas are eternal and, given simplicity, one reality.

keyTerms.definition: Knowing all truths whatsoever — necessary and contingent, possible and actual. The adjective is “omniscient.”
keyTerms.example: God knows not only that 2 + 2 = 4 but what you ate for breakfast.
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis, “all,” + scientia, “knowledge.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conceptual omniscience — which covers only essences, possibilities, and necessary truths.

keyTerms.definition: A logical relation in which the truth of some propositions guarantees the truth of another.
keyTerms.example: “All men are mortal” and “Socrates is a man” together entail “Socrates is mortal.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Dependence — A can entail B (or be entailed by it) without depending on B, as arithmetic entails truths about rocks.

keyTerms.definition: The view that concepts, logic, mathematics, and science are all products of contingent biological, social, historical, and cultural forces, with no necessary connection to objective reality.
keyTerms.example: Claiming that logic is merely a Western cultural product that another society could replace.
keyTerms.origin: A development of psychologism, as Feser describes it.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Recognizing cultural influence on how truths are expressed — sentences differ across cultures; propositions and logical relations do not.

keyTerms.definition: The less radical view, inspired by Kant, that our concepts and logic reflect only the structure of our minds rather than objective reality, but necessarily and unchangeably so.
keyTerms.example: Saying causality and number are forms our minds impose on experience, not features of things in themselves.
keyTerms.origin: Immanuel Kant (1724–1804), Critique of Pure Reason.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Radical relativism — the Kantian says our mental structure is fixed and universal, not culturally variable.

keyTerms.definition: The view that talk of numbers and other abstract objects is literally false but useful, like a good story.
keyTerms.example: “2 + 2 = 4” is true in the story of arithmetic the way “Sherlock lives on Baker Street” is true in Conan Doyle.
keyTerms.origin: A modern position (e.g., Hartry Field); Feser mentions “useful fictions” among the options realism rejects.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Formalism — which treats mathematics as a game of manipulating symbols by rules; both deny mathematical objects exist.

keyTerms.definition: In traditional theology, a disembodied intellect that does not perish but exists only because God creates it.
keyTerms.example: Feser uses a world containing only angels as a possible world with no matter or human minds.
keyTerms.origin: Greek angelos, “messenger.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: A necessary being — an angel never dies but still exists contingently, so it cannot ground necessary truths.

keyTerms.definition: The geometry of flat space built from Euclid’s axioms, in which, for example, the angles of every triangle add up to two right angles (180 degrees).
keyTerms.example: Feser qualifies the angle-sum truth: it holds “at least if it is Euclidean triangles we are talking about.”
keyTerms.origin: Euclid of Alexandria, Elements (c. 300 B.C.).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Non-Euclidean geometry — geometry of curved space, where angle sums differ; its truths are about different objects and do not refute Euclid’s.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever is capable of being true or false. For Feser, propositions are the primary truth-bearers; sentences are true only because they express true propositions.
keyTerms.example: The proposition that snow is white is a truth-bearer, expressed equally by “Snow is white” and “Schnee ist weiss.”
keyTerms.origin: Term from contemporary philosophy of language.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Truthmaker — the truth-bearer is what is true; the truthmaker is what in reality makes it true.

keyTerms.definition: The contemporary term for a thought or experience understood as a concrete, particular item — an event in the brain or in an immaterial soul.
keyTerms.example: Your belief, right now, that snow is white, considered as something happening in your head.
keyTerms.origin: Contemporary philosophy of mind.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The content of a thought — many different mental states (yours, mine, Socrates’) can have one and the same content, a proposition.

keyTerms.definition: A general statement of how things of certain kinds behave. Because it is general, it refers to universals — kinds and properties — rather than to any one particular thing.
keyTerms.example: The inverse-square law of gravity applies to every pair of masses, observed or not.
keyTerms.origin: Early modern science (Descartes, Newton); the metaphysics of laws is itself debated.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Logical or metaphysical necessity — the laws of physics could have been different in another possible world; 2 + 2 = 4 could not.

keyTerms.definition: Existing or holding regardless of whether some mind thinks of it. The crucial question is always *which* minds: independence from human minds is not the same as independence from every mind.
keyTerms.example: 2 + 2 = 4 is independent of human minds; on Scholastic realism it is not independent of the divine mind.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Independence from every mind — Feser’s direct arguments for realism establish only independence from matter and from finite minds; that gap is what the Scholastic exploits.

keyTerms.definition: The power of the mind to grasp universals (concepts), combine them into propositions, and reason from some propositions to others. On the Aristotelian view, the intellect takes on the form of a thing without its matter. “Intellectual” describes what belongs to this power.
keyTerms.example: Grasping triangularity, forming the thought that all men are mortal, and inferring that Socrates is mortal.
keyTerms.origin: Latin intellectus, from intelligere, “to understand.” Chapter 1 lists the three capacities.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Imagination or sensation — these deal with particular images; the intellect grasps what no image can capture, such as triangularity as such.

keyTerms.definition: The late ancient development of Plato’s philosophy, above all by Plotinus (3rd century A.D.), which placed the Forms within a divine Intellect that derives from an absolutely simple One. Adjective: Neo-Platonic.
keyTerms.example: Feser says the idea behind the Augustinian proof has roots in Neo-Platonic thought, which Augustine absorbed.
keyTerms.origin: Plotinus, Enneads; later Proclus. The subject of Feser’s Chapter 2.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Platonic realism — Plato’s Forms seem to exist apart from any mind; Neo-Platonists located them in Intellect.

keyTerms.definition: A set of propositions is consistent if they can all be true together, inconsistent if they cannot.
keyTerms.example: “All men are mortal” and “Cats are four-legged” are consistent; “Socrates is mortal” and “Socrates is not mortal” are inconsistent.
keyTerms.origin: Latin consistere, “to stand together.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Entailment — consistent propositions need not entail one another; they merely do not conflict.

keyTerms.definition: A chart showing how the truth value of a compound proposition (built with “and,” “or,” “not,” “if…then”) follows from the truth values of its parts.
keyTerms.example: “It is raining and it is cold” is true only if both parts are true.
keyTerms.origin: Popularized by Wittgenstein and Post (1921).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Probability — truth tables fix truth values from components; they do not measure likelihood.

keyTerms.definition: Having all power: the ability to actualize whatever can be actualized. The adjective is “omnipotent.” Feser derives it from pure actuality, which is the source of all actualizing power.
keyTerms.example: God could create a world with unicorns in it, since that is a possibility he knows — but not a round square, which is not a possible thing at all.
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis, “all,” + potentia, “power.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: The ability to do the self-contradictory — omnipotence does not include making 2 + 2 = 5, because that is not a “something” to be done.

keyTerms.definition: Complete goodness: for Feser, a thing is good to the extent it realizes its nature without defect (privation), so what is purely actual, lacking any privation, is good in the fullest sense.
keyTerms.example: A good painter is one who has actualized the skills painting requires; a purely actual being lacks nothing at all.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian and Thomistic tradition, in which goodness is tied to actuality; argued in Chapter 1.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Moral rule-following — this is goodness in the sense of complete perfection, not merely obeying moral duties.

keyTerms.definition: The absence of a feature that a thing ought by its nature to have in order to be complete — a failure to realize a potential.
keyTerms.example: A squirrel missing its tail, or a tree with weak roots (Feser’s Chapter 1 examples).
keyTerms.origin: Latin privatio, “deprivation.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere absence — a stone’s lacking sight is not a privation, because sight does not belong to a stone’s nature.

keyTerms.definition: Being unable to change. The adjective is “immutable.” It follows from pure actuality, since change is the actualization of a potential.
keyTerms.example: God does not come to learn a truth or acquire a new idea; he eternally understands everything.
keyTerms.origin: Latin in-, “not,” + mutare, “to change.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Causal inertness — an immutable God is the cause of everything; an inert Platonic Form causes nothing.

keyTerms.definition: Being immaterial means not being made of matter; being incorporeal means not having a body. Both follow from pure actuality, since matter involves potentiality.
keyTerms.example: God’s intellect is not a brain; numbers and propositions are also immaterial, though not in the same way.
keyTerms.origin: Latin materia, “matter,” and corpus, “body.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Unreality — immaterial things (numbers, minds, God) can be fully real.

keyTerms.definition: Existing without beginning, end, or succession of moments — outside time altogether. The adjective is “eternal.” It follows from immutability, since time involves change.
keyTerms.example: God does not learn that 2 + 2 = 4 at some moment; he understands it eternally.
keyTerms.origin: Latin aeternitas; classic definition in Boethius.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Everlastingness — lasting through endless time; an angel might never cease to exist yet still exist in time and contingently.

keyTerms.definition: The divine attribute that there is and can be only one God — only one purely actual being — because nothing could differentiate two of them.
keyTerms.example: Steps 20–21: a “committee” of necessary intellects collapses into one.
keyTerms.origin: Argued in Feser’s Chapter 1; discussed again in Chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Divine simplicity — unity says there is only one God; simplicity says God has no parts.

keyTerms.definition: Actuality is the way a thing actually is; potentiality is its real capacity to be otherwise; to actualize is to make a potential actual. From Chapter 1.
keyTerms.example: A student who has not studied calculus has a potential to know it; learning actualizes that potential.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s dunamis and energeia; Latin potentia and actus.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Logical possibility — a scenario can be possible even where no existing thing has a potential for it (e.g., a world possible before anything exists).

keyTerms.definition: The traditional conception of God, shared by thinkers such as Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, Maimonides, and Avicenna, as simple, immutable, eternal, necessary, purely actual, omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good.
keyTerms.example: Step 28: the list of attributes reached in step 27 is “what it is for God to exist” in classical theism.
keyTerms.origin: Name used by Feser and others for the mainstream tradition of philosophical theology.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Theistic personalism — a view (criticized by Feser in Chapter 6) that models God as a person like us but greater, sometimes changeable or composite.

keyTerms.term: Argument by elimination (disjunctive syllogism, modus tollens)
keyTerms.definition: Two basic valid argument forms. Disjunctive syllogism: from “A or B or C” and “not A” and “not B,” infer C. Modus tollens: from “if P then Q” and “not Q,” infer “not P.”
keyTerms.example: Steps 11 and 13 use modus tollens; step 14 uses disjunctive syllogism to conclude Scholastic realism.
keyTerms.origin: Stoic logic; Latin names from medieval logic.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Begging the question — an elimination argument is only as good as its premises that the options are exhaustive and that the others fail.

keyTerms.definition: The logical rule that “if P then Q” is equivalent to “if not-Q then not-P.”
keyTerms.example: Leftow contraposes “If God exists, water is necessarily H₂O” into “If water is not necessarily H₂O, God does not exist.”
keyTerms.origin: Traditional logic.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The converse (“if Q then P”), which is not equivalent — and dependence, which contraposition does not show.

keyTerms.definition: A truth that is necessary but can be known only through experience rather than by pure reasoning. In contemporary philosophy “water = H₂O” is the standard example.
keyTerms.example: No one could work out by thought alone that water is H₂O, yet (on this view) water could not have been anything else.
keyTerms.origin: Latin a posteriori, “from what comes after” (experience); made prominent by Saul Kripke (1970).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Contingent truth — the fact that we learn something by experience does not make it contingent.

keyTerms.definition: In contemporary usage: existing in space and time with causal powers. In Aristotelian-Scholastic usage: a nature as it exists in an individual thing, bound up with individuating features, as opposed to that nature considered in abstraction by an intellect.
keyTerms.example: Humanness exists concretely in Socrates and abstractly in your intellect when you think about humanity.
keyTerms.origin: Latin concretus, “grown together.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Material — something could be concrete (a particular) without being material, e.g., an immaterial soul on a Cartesian view.

keyTerms.definition: René Descartes’ view that the mind is an immaterial thinking thing, distinct from the body, whose thoughts are its states.
keyTerms.example: Some critics picture divine ideas as the concrete states of a Cartesian-style mind — a picture Feser says the Scholastic rejects.
keyTerms.origin: René Descartes (1596–1650), Meditations.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Aristotelian intellect — a power of the soul that receives forms without matter, not a separate thing with a stream of particular states.

keyTerms.definition: The view that science is the only source of genuine knowledge.
keyTerms.example: Saying “only what can be empirically tested is knowable” — a claim that itself cannot be empirically tested.
keyTerms.origin: 20th-century term, often critical.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Science — scientism is a philosophical thesis about science, not a result of science.

keyTerms.definition: The view that necessary truths are true merely because of linguistic conventions — how we have chosen to use words and symbols.
keyTerms.example: “2 + 2 = 4 is true only because of how we defined ‘2,’ ‘+,’ and ‘4.’”
keyTerms.origin: Logical positivism (e.g., Carnap, Ayer); rebutted in Feser’s Chapter 6 with reference to this chapter.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The conventionality of notation — which symbols express a proposition is conventional; whether the proposition is necessary is not.

keyTerms.definition: The challenge of explaining how we could know anything about abstract objects if they are causally inert and outside space and time.
keyTerms.example: If the number 7 never affects your brain, how did you come to know that 7 is prime?
keyTerms.origin: Paul Benacerraf, “Mathematical Truth” (1973).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Feser’s causal-inertness objection — closely related, but Feser adds the further problem that inert Forms could not explain why particulars conform to them.

keyTerms.definition: The view that mathematics is the manipulation of symbols according to rules, not a body of truths about real objects.
keyTerms.example: Treating arithmetic like chess: moves are allowed or disallowed, but nothing is “true” about numbers.
keyTerms.origin: Associated with David Hilbert’s program and later thinkers.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Fictionalism — which says mathematical statements are false but useful stories; formalism says they are rule-governed moves.

keyTerms.definition: The Scholastic principle that whatever is in an effect must in some way be in its cause — formally, or in a higher (eminent) way.
keyTerms.example: Chapter 6 uses it: every form found in things must exist in God, and since not as it is in things, it exists as an idea in his intellect.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic philosophy; discussed in Feser’s Chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: “Like causes like” in a crude sense — God need not be red to cause red things.

keyTerms.definition: Existence is the fact *that* a thing is, as opposed to its essence, *what* it is. The distinction is the starting point of Feser’s Chapter 4.
keyTerms.example: You can know what a unicorn is without knowing whether any unicorn exists.
keyTerms.origin: Avicenna and Aquinas; Latin esse, “to be.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Essence — what a thing is, which can be grasped without knowing that it is.

keyTerms.term: Per se vs. per accidens causal series
keyTerms.definition: From Chapter 1: in a per se (hierarchical) series, each member’s causal activity depends here and now on a prior member; in a per accidens (linear) series, earlier members need not still exist or act. The Augustinian proof does not use this distinction, since it is not causal.
keyTerms.example: Per se: a hand moving a stick moving a stone. Per accidens: a grandfather, father, and son.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic terminology (Aquinas).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Temporal vs. timeless causes — the key is dependence of causal power, not time.

keyTerms.definition: A collection of objects treated as a single mathematical object; a subset is a set all of whose members belong to another set.
keyTerms.example: {2, 4} is a subset of {1, 2, 3, 4}; the power set of {a, b} is {∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}}.
keyTerms.origin: Georg Cantor’s set theory (late 19th century).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Plurality — we can speak about “all propositions” without supposing they form a set.

keyTerms.definition: The property of standing for or being about something else. Thoughts, propositions, maps, and pictures represent; stones do not.
keyTerms.example: The proposition that all men are mortal is about men; a drawing of Socrates hammering nails is about Socrates.
keyTerms.origin: Closely tied to “intentionality” (Brentano).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Resemblance — a picture may resemble what it represents, but a sentence represents without resembling.

keyTerms.definition: An infinite series of explanations in which each step depends on the next to do its explaining, so the explanation is never actually completed. An infinite series is not bad in itself; it is vicious when it postpones the explanation forever.
keyTerms.example: Russell’s regress: explaining red things by resemblance, resemblances by higher resemblances, and so on, never explains what the resemblances share.
keyTerms.origin: Latin regressus, “a going back.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: A harmless infinite series — such as “p,” “it is true that p,” “it is true that it is true that p” — where no step depends on the next for its explanation.

keyTerms.definition: Arguing in a way that assumes the very point in dispute, so that a premise can be accepted only by someone who already accepts the conclusion.
keyTerms.example: Coffey charges the Augustinian argument with it; Feser replies that atheist Platonists accept the key premise, so it assumes nothing about God.
keyTerms.origin: Latin petitio principii, “assuming the starting point.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Raising the question — in ordinary speech “begs the question” often means “invites the question,” which is a different sense.

keyTerms.definition: The features that make a particular thing this individual rather than another of the same kind — its matter, location, size, color, and so on. Abstraction sets them aside.
keyTerms.example: This triangle is wooden and green, that one stone and orange; triangularity ignores such differences.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic “principle of individuation,” debated since Boethius and Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Essence — the essence is what individuals of a kind share; individuating features are what distinguish them.

keyTerms.definition: The basic valid argument form: from “if P then Q” and “P,” infer “Q.”
keyTerms.example: If all men are mortal and Socrates is a man, then Socrates is mortal (a closely related syllogism).
keyTerms.origin: Latin, “the mode that affirms.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Affirming the consequent — from “if P then Q” and “Q,” inferring “P,” which is invalid.

keyTerms.definition: In a conditional “if P then Q,” P is the antecedent and Q the consequent. A conditional with an impossible antecedent describes no genuine scenario.
keyTerms.example: In Leftow’s “if it were not necessary that water = H₂O, God would not exist,” the antecedent is the “if” clause about water.
keyTerms.origin: Traditional logic; Latin antecedens, “going before.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Cause and effect — the antecedent need not cause the consequent; the relation is logical.

keyTerms.definition: A general feature (a determinable) leaves certain specifications open; an existing individual is fully determinate — it is definitely one way or the other in every relevant respect.
keyTerms.example: Animality leaves open rational or nonrational, but every actual animal is determinately one or the other — the heart of the animality problem.
keyTerms.origin: Terminology from W. E. Johnson (1921); the idea is ancient.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Vagueness — a universal is not vague; it is precisely general.

keyTerms.definition: The truth or falsity of a proposition.
keyTerms.example: The truth value of “snow is white” is true; that of “2 + 2 = 5” is false.
keyTerms.origin: Frege.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Truthmaker — the truth value is whether a proposition is true; the truthmaker is what makes it so.

distinctions.name: Sentence (or numeral) vs. proposition (or number)

left.label: Sentence / numeral
left.desc: A physical or spoken token in a particular language or notation; visible, erasable, located in space and time; different in English, German, Arabic, Roman.

right.label: Proposition / number
right.desc: The abstract content the token expresses or names; shared across languages and centuries; cannot be seen or erased; its truth survives the destruction of every token.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This is the doorway into the whole chapter. Once someone sees that destroying every copy of “2 + 2 = 4” would not make it false, they are forced to ask what kind of thing it is — and physical or linguistic answers are ruled out.

distinctions.name: Nominalism vs. conceptualism

left.label: Nominalism
left.desc: Denies that universals and other abstract objects are real at all: there are only particular things and general words or resemblances.

right.label: Conceptualism
right.desc: Grants that universals are real but says they exist only as constructs of human minds, with no foundation outside them.

distinctions.whyItMatters: They fail in different ways. Nominalism is refuted by the regress of resemblance and by the fact that its own words are universals. Conceptualism is refuted by shared concepts, communication, and the self-refuting character of psychologism. You must know which rival you are facing to use the right argument.

distinctions.name: Platonic vs. Aristotelian realism

left.label: Platonic realism
left.desc: Universals exist as abstract and mind-independent at once — Forms in a third realm outside space, time, and minds; things only imperfectly resemble them.

right.label: Aristotelian realism
right.desc: Universals exist mind-independently only in concrete things (tied to individuating features) and exist as abstract only in an intellect that abstracts them; there is no third way of existing.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Feser’s whole argument turns on rejecting the idea that anything can be both abstract and mind-independent. Once that is granted, abstract objects need a mind — and the question becomes which mind.

distinctions.name: Aristotelian vs. Scholastic realism

left.label: Aristotelian (finite minds only)
left.desc: Abstract objects exist in things and in human or other contingent intellects — nothing more.

right.label: Scholastic realism
right.desc: Agrees with Aristotle against a mindless third realm, but agrees with Plato that there must be a realm beyond matter and finite minds: a necessary, divine intellect.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The step from Aristotelian to Scholastic realism is where God enters. It is justified by the four hard cases — possibility with no world, pure possibles, propositions true without minds, and necessary truths — which contingent minds cannot ground.

distinctions.name: Contemporary vs. Scholastic understanding of “abstract”

left.label: Contemporary
left.desc: Abstract means outside the spatiotemporal order; everything is either abstract or concrete, full stop; thoughts are concrete mental states in brains or souls.

right.label: Aristotelian-Scholastic
right.desc: Abstract means produced by the intellect’s act of abstraction; the same nature (humanness, redness) exists concretely in things and abstractly in an intellect; to think is to take on a form without its matter.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This dissolves the objection that divine ideas would be “concrete, not abstract.” The objection assumes the contemporary definition, which the Scholastic rejects; pressing it simply begs the question.

distinctions.name: Conceptual omniscience vs. unqualified omniscience

left.label: Conceptual omniscience
left.desc: Knowing all essences, possibilities, and necessary truths — what the interlocking-system argument directly delivers.

right.label: Unqualified omniscience
right.desc: Knowing all truths whatsoever, including contingent ones about what actually happens.

distinctions.whyItMatters: A skeptic can grant the first and deny the second. Feser closes the gap through pure actuality: ignorance of any truth is an unactualized potential. (And the actual is a subset of the possible.) This is the bridge to the fuller treatment of omniscience in Chapter 6.

distinctions.name: Logical entailment vs. real dependence

left.label: Entailment
left.desc: If A necessarily implies B, then by contraposition not-B implies not-A — a purely logical relation that holds among necessary truths in every direction.

right.label: Dependence
right.desc: A genuine explanatory relation in which one thing exists or holds because of another, so that changes in the second could overturn the first.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Leftow’s water objection trades on confusing the two. Arithmetic entails truths about rocks without depending on rocks; the divine nature entails truths about water without depending on water.

illustrations.title: The pool hall
illustrations.body:
Feser’s opening scene. Everything on the table is a particular — this cue, that eight ball, this rack. But ask what the cues have in common, and you are no longer talking about any one of them: you are talking about *being a pool cue*. Ask what the red balls share with fire engines and strawberries, and you have reached **redness**; what the rack shares with pyramids and dunce caps, **triangularity**.

Use it to make the audience notice that ordinary talk constantly refers to things no one can put on a table. The pool hall is concrete; the patterns it displays are not.

illustrations.title: Erasing every “Snow is white” (and every “2”)
illustrations.body:
Write “Snow is white” on a whiteboard. You can see the sentence; you cannot see the proposition — the same one is expressed by “Schnee ist weiss,” which looks nothing like it. Now imagine erasing every token of that sentence in every language on earth. Would it stop being true that snow is white? Of course not. The same goes for numbers: burn every “2” and every “II” ever written, and 2 + 2 = 4 is untouched.

The move to make: whatever a proposition or a number is, it is not ink, sound, or pixels. And Socrates in Athens and Obama in Washington can think the *very same* proposition in different languages 2,500 years apart — so it is not locked inside any one head either.

illustrations.title: The architect versus the inert Form
illustrations.body:
A wooden rack pushes balls into a triangle. A dinner bell, rung, makes a sound. An architect, holding the concept of triangularity, designs a pyramid that takes that shape. In every case where triangularity *does* anything, it is either in a material thing or in a mind.

Now picture Plato’s Form of Triangle: in no thing, in no mind, outside space and time. What could it do? If it affects nothing, it does not affect us — so how do we know about it? And it does not affect actual triangles — so how does it explain why they are triangular? The illustration shows why Feser thinks abstract objects belong in minds, where representations actually have effects.

illustrations.title: Animality: neither rational nor nonrational
illustrations.body:
Every actual animal is either rational (a human) or nonrational (a dog, a horse). Animality itself must cover both, so it cannot contain rationality (dogs would be excluded) or nonrationality (humans would be excluded). In itself it is *neither*. But nothing that exists as an individual thing can be neither rational nor nonrational.

Conclusion: animality, considered as such, cannot exist as a thing in its own right — it cannot be a Platonic Form. It can exist only *in* animals (always tied to one or the other) or *as abstracted* in an intellect. This is the argument Feser rates as more telling than the famous Third Man.

illustrations.title: The tree and its mirror image
illustrations.body:
On Plato’s view, what makes a tree a tree is not in the tree but in the Form of Tree, which the tree merely imitates. But then the oak in your yard is related to treeness in the same way a statue or a reflection of a tree is — an image of something located elsewhere. Your oak would be no more genuinely a tree than its reflection in a pond.

That is absurd, and it shows why the Aristotelian insists that natures are *in* things — trees are substances with their own intrinsic principles — and exist as abstract only when a mind abstracts them.

illustrations.title: Socrates the carpenter (Welty’s drawing)
illustrations.body:
Draw Socrates hammering nails. The drawing represents a possibility: Socrates might have been a carpenter. But no one thinks the drawing *makes* that possible — as if Socrates could not have been a carpenter had the drawing never been made. A Platonic “possible world” in a third realm is in the same position as the drawing: a representation with no connection to what could actually happen.

The Scholastic alternative: the possibility is an idea in the mind of an omniscient and omnipotent cause who *could have made* such a world following that idea. Now the representation is relevant, because it belongs to someone with the power to realize it.

illustrations.title: Two rocks plus two rocks
illustrations.body:
Feser’s parallel to Leftow’s water objection. Because 2 + 2 = 4 is necessary, it is necessary that two rocks plus two rocks make four rocks. Contrapose, and you can say: if that rock truth were not necessary, neither would 2 + 2 = 4 be. Does arithmetic therefore “depend on rocks”? No — mineralogy is never going to overturn arithmetic.

So too: the divine nature entails that water is necessarily H₂O, but hydrology will never overturn God. Logical entailment running backward is not dependence.

illustrations.title: The crossword that can’t be split
illustrations.body:
Imagine trying to divide a completed crossword puzzle among several people, each keeping only some of the words. It cannot be done cleanly: every across answer shares letters with down answers, which share letters with other across answers. To hold any word *as part of this puzzle*, you have to hold its crossings — and theirs.

The realm of eternal truths is like that, only infinitely larger. Humanness crosses animality and rationality; propositions cross universals; every proposition is consistent or inconsistent with every other. That is why Feser concludes there cannot be a committee of necessary minds each holding a portion: the whole interlocking system has to be in one mind.

illustrations.title: The architect’s blueprints (the key analogy)
illustrations.body:
Before a building exists, where is it? In the architect’s mind, as a plan. The plan is *about* the building (it represents), it is *real* before any brick is laid, and it is *relevant* to what can be built, because it belongs to someone with the power to build it. Plans that no one has ever thought of do not exist anywhere at all.

The Augustinian proof says the eternal truths — every essence, every possibility, every necessary truth — are like that: plans in the mind of One who needs no one else to exist and who could bring any of them about. Unlike a human architect, this mind cannot fail to exist, cannot forget, and never began, which is why the truths it holds are necessary and eternal. Use this to show at once why abstract objects need a mind (intentionality), why the mind must be necessary (the truths are necessary), and why the mind must be powerful (relevance).

objections.title: Divine ideas would be concrete, not abstract
objections.whoRaises: Keith Yandell, William Lane Craig (in replies to Welty); many contemporary analytic metaphysicians
objections.objection: Abstract objects, by definition, are non-mental entities outside space and time with no causal powers. If universals, propositions, and possible worlds are really thoughts in God’s mind, they are concrete mental items, not abstract objects. So Scholastic realism does not account for abstract objects at all — it simply replaces them with something else.
objections.reply:
1. There is no consensus, even among contemporary metaphysicians, about what abstract objects are (Welty’s point), so there is no settled, neutral definition that puts the burden of proof on the Scholastic.
2. Even if there were a consensus, the objection would beg the question. For the Aristotelian and Scholastic, an abstract object just *is* what an intellect forms by abstracting from particulars. The critic says abstract objects cannot be in an intellect; the Scholastic says they can *only* be in an intellect. Asserting the first does nothing to show the second false.
3. Underneath lie two different pictures. Moderns think of thought as a concrete “mental state” in a brain or Cartesian soul, and draw the abstract/concrete line as outside versus inside space and time. Scholastics think of thought as receiving a form without its matter, and hold that one and the same nature can exist concretely in things and abstractly in an intellect.
objections.pushback: If the objector insists “but God’s thoughts are still particular events in a particular mind,” point out that on divine simplicity God’s thought is not a series of events or a particular state among others; it is not in time, not a part of God, and not one item among many. The objector is applying a model of human mental states that the argument explicitly rejects. Ask what, exactly, is lost: the divine ideas are universal in content, necessary, eternal, and non-physical — everything the Platonist wanted from abstract objects, minus the mysterious mindless realm.

objections.title: Leftow: God’s existence would depend on facts about water
objections.objection: On a “deity theory,” all necessities flow from God’s nature. Suppose water = H₂O is necessary. Then God’s nature entails that water = H₂O necessarily. By contraposition, if water were not necessarily H₂O, God would not exist. So God’s very existence would hang on facts about water — which is absurd. Deity theories should be restricted to logic and mathematics.
objections.reply:
1. Run the same pattern on arithmetic: 2 + 2 = 4 entails that two rocks plus two rocks necessarily make four rocks, so if that were not necessary, 2 + 2 = 4 would not be necessary. No one concludes that arithmetic *depends* on rocks. Necessary truths entail necessary consequences about everything; entailment is not dependence, and mineralogy will never overturn arithmetic.
2. Likewise the divine nature entails necessary truths about water, and hydrology will never overturn God. Leftow does not claim it could — but then what does the counterintuitive “dependence” amount to?
3. The antecedent “if it were not necessary that water = H₂O” describes no genuine scenario. Just as one should refuse to “consider a scenario in which 2 + 2 does not necessarily equal 4,” the deity theorist may refuse to consider this one (following Welty).
4. Leftow’s voluntarism — the necessity comes from God’s will, so God could have willed otherwise — just begs the question against deity theorists, who reject voluntarism.
objections.pushback: If pressed that water = H₂O is an a posteriori necessity and so feels more “contingent” than arithmetic, reply that how we *learn* a truth does not settle whether it is necessary. If it is necessary at all, the same logic applies; if it is not necessary, then the objection never gets started, since the deity theory only needs to ground genuine necessities.

objections.title: Grim: Cantor’s theorem rules out omniscience
objections.objection: A conceptually omniscient being would have to know the set of all truths. But there can be no such set: take any set S of truths; by Cantor’s theorem its power set is larger, and each subset generates a further truth not in S. So no set contains all truths, and the idea of omniscience is incoherent.
objections.reply:
1. **It proves too much** (Plantinga). The same reasoning shows there is no set of all propositions whatsoever — yet we coherently assert things about all propositions (every one is true or false; none is both). So why can we not coherently say an omniscient being knows all true propositions?
2. **No set needed** (Simmons). Omniscience means there is no proposition God fails to know. Even if the truths do not form a set, it does not follow that any particular truth is unknown to God.
3. **Simplicity** (Wainwright). Grim pictures divine knowledge as a collection of discrete ideas forming a set. But on divine simplicity, what we describe as God’s many distinct “grasps” of propositions is one and the same reality in God, described in different ways.
objections.pushback: If the objector says “without a set, ‘all truths’ is meaningless,” ask whether he thinks “every proposition is either true or false” is meaningless. Quantifying over everything does not require a set-theoretic collection — logicians and mathematicians do it constantly (classes, plural quantification). The objection targets a particular formal model of knowledge, not omniscience itself.

objections.title: Coffey: the argument begs the question
objections.whoRaises: Peter Coffey (and Mercier’s Manual) — Scholastics who accept Scholastic realism but deny it can prove God
objections.objection: The argument assumes that possibilities are eternally and necessarily possible — that unicorns were possible before any world or finite mind. But how could we know that unless we already knew there is a necessary intellect to ground it? And the idea of an order of abstract objects independent of our minds is a Platonic illusion. Either you mean a Platonic realm (false) or a divine mind (question-begging).
objections.reply:
1. Even an **atheist** Platonist agrees that possibilities are eternal and necessary. So one does *not* need to presuppose a divine intellect to accept this premise.
2. Coffey himself, as a Scholastic realist, believes an order of abstract objects independent of finite minds really exists — in God. So it cannot be wholly illusory; only the Platonic *interpretation* of it could be.
3. The dilemma (Platonic or divine) is a **false choice**. One can affirm that there is an order of abstract objects existing *in some way* independently of all finite minds while leaving open *what* way. That is exactly the common ground on which Platonists and Scholastics argue. Accepting it without (a) means assuming nothing false; accepting it without (b) means begging no question.
objections.pushback: If someone repeats “but you are only confident possibilities are eternal because you believe in God,” ask them directly: before any human existed, was it possible for humans to exist? Nearly everyone says yes. That intuition is shared by theists and atheists alike and is the argument’s real starting point.

objections.title: Why not several necessary minds — a committee?
objections.whoRaises: A critic Feser anticipates in Stage 2; also polytheists or pluralists
objections.objection: Grant that abstract objects need a necessary intellect. Why only one? Perhaps necessary mind A holds some possible worlds and truths, necessary mind B holds others, and so on.
objections.reply:
1. Abstract objects form an **interlocking system**: grasping one universal requires grasping those that define it; propositions are built from universals; every proposition is logically related to every other (entailment, consistency, truth-functional combination). These relations hold independently of any world or finite mind, so whatever mind grounds them must grasp them *all* — you cannot hold one strand without the web.
2. More fundamentally, a necessarily existing intellect must be **purely actual** (otherwise its existence would depend on some potential being actualized), and there cannot be two purely actual things, since nothing could differentiate them (Chapter 1).
objections.pushback: If the critic suggests two minds each holding the *whole* system, the pure-actuality argument answers it: two such minds would have to differ in something — some feature or perfection one has and the other lacks — and pure actuality admits no such difference. Two “identical” necessary minds collapse into one.

objections.title: A cosmic mathematician is not God
objections.whoRaises: A critic Feser anticipates (echoing Robert Adams’s caution); typical skeptic
objections.objection: At best you have a mind that knows all necessary truths and possibilities — a kind of eternal logician. Why think it knows contingent facts, has power, cares about goodness, or deserves the name “God”?
objections.reply:
1. An intellect that exists of absolute necessity must be purely actual; if its existence presupposed the actualization of any potential, it would be contingent.
2. Chapter 1 showed that what is purely actual is unique, omnipotent (the source of all actualizing power), perfectly good (no privation), immutable, immaterial, incorporeal, and eternal.
3. It must know contingent truths too: to lack any knowledge is to have an unactualized potential to know. And the actual is a subset of the possible, so knowing all possible truths already includes the actual ones.
4. Welty’s relevance point adds that possibilities are real possibilities precisely because they are ideas in a mind that has the power to actualize them.
objections.pushback: If the skeptic rejects pure actuality, show the link concretely: a being that could exist only if some potential were actualized would owe its existence to whatever actualizes it — and then it is not the ultimate, necessary ground. The necessity the argument needs is incompatible with any unactualized potential. This is exactly why Chapter 1 and Chapter 3 converge on the same God.

objections.title: Why not a mind-independent Platonic realm?
objections.whoRaises: Contemporary mathematical Platonists (e.g., many working mathematicians and analytic philosophers)
objections.objection: Grant realism. The simplest view is that numbers, propositions, and possible worlds just exist, necessarily and eternally, on their own — no mind required. Causal inertness is no problem: mathematical knowledge does not work by causal contact anyway. Adding a mind is an unnecessary theological extra.
objections.reply:
1. **Inertness.** If third-realm objects affect nothing, they do not affect particular things either — so they cannot explain why this rack is triangular — and it becomes mysterious how minds could know about them at all.
2. **The animality problem.** A universal like animality must be neither rational nor nonrational, but nothing existing as an individual in its own right can be that. So universals cannot exist as self-standing objects.
3. **Essences exiled from things** would make trees no more treelike than reflections.
4. **Welty’s conditions.** Abstract objects *represent* (a proposition is about something), and representation is at home in minds, not in a mindless realm; a third realm adds a whole extra category of being (simplicity); and a third-realm possible world is no better a truthmaker for what could happen than a drawing is (relevance).
objections.pushback: If the Platonist says “representation needn’t involve a mind,” ask for one example of something that is *intrinsically* about something else without deriving its aboutness from a mind. Words, maps, and drawings all borrow their meaning from minds. Propositions are the paradigm of intrinsic aboutness — exactly what thoughts have. The burden is on the Platonist to explain mindless aboutness.

objections.title: It’s just words: resemblance nominalism
objections.whoRaises: Nominalists, from medieval Ockhamists to contemporary resemblance nominalists
objections.objection: There is no “redness.” There are red things, and there is the word “red,” which we apply to things that resemble one another. Talk of universals is a trick of language.
objections.reply:
1. Why do we apply “red” to just these things? “Because they share redness” brings universals back; “because they resemble each other” — in what respect? Obviously in their redness.
2. **Russell’s regress.** Resemblance is itself a universal, instantiated by the stop sign/fire truck pair, the grass/Hulk pair, and so on. Treat those resemblances as merely resembling each other and you need a higher-order resemblance, and so on forever.
3. **Words are universals too.** “Red” said by you, me, and Socrates is one word type with many tokens. If instead each utterance is a merely resembling word, no one ever uses the same word twice, communication becomes impossible — and the nominalist cannot even state his view to us.
objections.pushback: If the nominalist takes resemblance as a primitive, unanalyzable relation, point out that he has now admitted one real universal (resemblance) that holds across countless pairs — the very thing he set out to deny. Once one universal is admitted, the principled objection to others is gone.

objections.title: Evolution and culture explain our logic and math
objections.whoRaises: Evolutionary naturalists, cultural relativists, heirs of psychologism
objections.objection: Our concepts, logical rules, and mathematics are products of how evolution and culture shaped human brains. They are useful, but they do not describe mind-independent reality; they describe how we are wired. No need for eternal truths, let alone an eternal mind.
objections.reply:
1. To state and defend this theory you must appeal to universals (selection pressure, mutation, social trend), to scientific and mathematical laws governing these processes, and to logical standards of good argument — the very things the theory says have no objective validity and did not exist before our minds. It saws off the branch it sits on.
2. The Kantian retreat (“our minds are necessarily structured this way”) faces a dilemma: either the theorist’s concepts and logic have no objective validity, and he cannot defend his view; or they do give him knowledge of the objective structure of minds, and he contradicts his view.
3. Shared concepts and communication across languages and millennia show concepts are not private products of individual brains.
objections.pushback: If the objector says evolution selected for *reliable* reasoning, thank them: reliability means our logic and math track something objective. Then the question returns — what is the objective reality that 2 + 2 = 4 is reliably tracking, which held before brains existed?

objections.title: Mathematics is a useful fiction (or a formal game)
objections.whoRaises: Mathematical fictionalists and formalists (a modern objection the chapter equips you to answer)
objections.objection: Numbers don’t exist. Mathematics is like a well-crafted story or a game of symbols: “2 + 2 = 4” is true in the story the way “Sherlock lives on Baker Street” is true in Conan Doyle. It is useful for science, but it commits us to nothing real.
objections.reply:
Feser lists “useful fictions” among the options realism rejects, and his direct arguments apply:

1. **Discovery, not invention.** Geometry and arithmetic yield truths we discover and cannot alter; fictions are invented and could have been written otherwise.
2. **Necessity and timelessness.** 2 + 2 = 4 was true before any storyteller existed and would remain true if all storytellers vanished; no fiction is like that.
3. **Science.** Science seeks objective, mind-independent facts and is formulated in mathematics and universal laws. If the mathematics is fiction, so is the physics that essentially uses it.
4. **Infinity.** The number series outruns every finite set of human ideas, so it cannot be a story humans have told.
objections.pushback: Ask the fictionalist: in the “story” of arithmetic, could the author have written that 2 + 2 = 5 without inconsistency? If not, what constrains the author — something about the story, or something the author is answerable to? The constraint is exactly what the realist is pointing at.

objections.title: Necessity and possibility need no ground
objections.whoRaises: Contemporary philosophers who treat modal facts as brute, or reduce possibility to mere logical consistency
objections.objection: “Possible” just means “logically consistent,” and necessary truths are simply the ones whose denial is contradictory. That is a fact about logic, not about any thing. Asking what grounds 2 + 2 = 4 is like asking what holds up the number line. It needs no ground and no location.
objections.reply:
1. Consistency is itself a *relation among propositions*, and propositions are among the abstract objects whose status is in question. Saying “it’s just logic” relocates the question rather than answering it: what kind of reality do these propositions and their logical relations have?
2. The options are exhausted by Feser’s analysis: denying that they are real (nominalism), making them human products (conceptualism), placing them in a third realm (Platonism), or placing them in an intellect. “Brute” modal facts that are real, necessary, and representational but in no mind are simply Platonism under another name — and inherit its problems.
3. The relevance point: a brute fact that “unicorns are possible” floating nowhere is no better a truthmaker than Welty’s drawing. A divine idea backed by power actually connects the possibility to what could be.
objections.pushback: If the objector says “some things are just brute,” ask whether *truths* can be brute in the sense of being true without being thought by anyone and without being about anything that grounds them. Truth is naturally a property of what is thought or asserted. The objector owes an account of truth-bearers that exist without any mind — which is the Platonist’s burden again.

misconceptions.myth: The Augustinian proof is another first-cause argument: God caused the laws of math.
misconceptions.correction: Feser stresses that it is the one proof in the book that is *not* causal. It does not argue that something produced 2 + 2 = 4; it argues that necessary, eternal truths can only exist as ideas in a necessary, eternal intellect. That is why the “What caused God?” objection is irrelevant to it.

misconceptions.myth: This is a Platonist argument — it says Plato was right about the Forms.
misconceptions.correction: It explicitly rejects Platonic realism’s mind-independent third realm. Scholastic realism is Aristotelian in spirit; it only grants Plato that there must be a reality beyond matter and finite minds — and identifies it as a divine intellect, not a realm of Forms.

misconceptions.myth: The argument says God makes up logic and mathematics by arbitrary decree, so he could have made 2 + 2 = 5.
misconceptions.correction: That is voluntarism, which Scholastic realists reject (see the reply to Leftow). Necessary truths are grounded in God’s intellect and nature, which are identical given divine simplicity, not in arbitrary choices. God could no more make 2 + 2 = 5 than he could cease to be God.

misconceptions.myth: Aristotelian realism is just conceptualism — universals are only in our heads.
misconceptions.correction: For the Aristotelian, universals really exist in things (tied to individuating features); the mind abstracts them *from* things rather than inventing them. Only *as abstract* do they exist solely in a mind. That is why Aristotelian realism counts as realism.

misconceptions.myth: The argument claims you must believe in God to know that 2 + 2 = 4.
misconceptions.correction: The argument is about what *grounds* the existence of necessary truths, not about how we come to know them. Atheists know mathematics perfectly well — indeed, the argument starts from truths everyone already knows.

misconceptions.myth: “Possible worlds” are other universes, like in a multiverse.
misconceptions.correction: A possible world is simply a way things could have been — Mars with three moons, Romney winning in 2012. It is an abstract object we reason about, not a physical place one could travel to.

misconceptions.myth: The argument only proves a cosmic logician, not the God of theism.
misconceptions.correction: Stage 2 goes further: a necessarily existing intellect must be purely actual, and by Chapter 1’s reasoning that entails uniqueness, omnipotence, perfect goodness, immutability, immateriality, eternity, and full (not just conceptual) omniscience.

misconceptions.myth: God’s mind is like a vast library holding infinitely many separate idea-files.
misconceptions.correction: Given divine simplicity, what we describe as many distinct ideas in God is really one and the same reality described in different ways. This matters for answering Grim’s set-theoretic objection.

misconceptions.myth: Humanity as a whole, or future civilizations, could collectively ground eternal truths.
misconceptions.correction: Any collection of contingent minds — human, extraterrestrial, even angelic — could have failed to exist and began to exist. Truths that held before them and would hold without them cannot depend on them. Only a necessarily existing intellect will do.

misconceptions.myth: Feser treats the Third Man as the knockout objection to Plato.
misconceptions.correction: He notes its force has been disputed for millennia and calls the animality problem more telling: a universal must be neither rational nor nonrational, but no individual can be.

misconceptions.myth: Conceptual omniscience is the same thing as full omniscience.
misconceptions.correction: Conceptual omniscience covers essences, possibilities, and necessary truths. Feser needs a further step — pure actuality rules out the potential to know more — to get knowledge of all contingent truths.

misconceptions.myth: Scholastic realism denies that universals exist in things or in human minds.
misconceptions.correction: It affirms both: universals exist concretely in things and abstractly in human and other finite intellects (step 9). It adds that they also, and ultimately, exist in a necessary divine intellect.

explain.twoMinute:
Start with something you already believe: some things are true no matter what. Two plus two is four. The angles of a Euclidean triangle add up to two right angles. Those truths were true before any human being existed, and they’d stay true if the universe blew up tomorrow.

Now ask: what *are* they? They’re not physical. You can erase every “2” ever written and arithmetic is untouched. They’re not just words — a German and an ancient Greek can think the exact same thought. And they’re not just ideas in our heads: we discovered them, we can’t change them, and you and I share them rather than each having a private version. Philosophers call things like this — numbers, propositions, universals like triangularity, possibilities — abstract objects. Trying to deny they’re real, or to make them human inventions, ends up using them in the very act of denying them.

So they’re real. But where? Plato said: in a third realm that’s neither physical nor mental. The trouble is that such things couldn’t do anything, couldn’t explain why actual triangles are triangular, and couldn’t be known. And there’s a deeper point: a truth is *about* something — it represents — and representing is what thoughts do. Abstract things exist abstractly only when a mind abstracts them.

So these truths live in a mind. Not a human mind — we come and go, and these truths didn’t wait for us. Not any created mind. It has to be a mind that exists necessarily, that couldn’t not exist. And because all these truths are interlocked — every proposition logically related to every other, infinitely — it has to be one mind grasping them all.

Finally, a mind that exists necessarily can’t have any unrealized potential, or its existence would depend on that potential being actualized. And something with no unrealized potential is one, all-powerful, perfectly good, unchanging, eternal — and knows everything. That’s not a cosmic calculator. That’s God.
explain.eli12:
Imagine you wrote “2 + 2 = 4” on every piece of paper in the world, and then burned all the paper. Would two plus two stop being four? No way! So two plus two equals four isn’t really made of paper or ink.

Is it just in our heads? Well, it was true before any people were born, and it would still be true if all people disappeared. And you and your friend in another country think the very same “two plus two is four,” not two different ones. So it’s not just in anybody’s head.

Some people say it floats around in a special invisible world all by itself. But ideas and truths are things that are *thought*. A truth that nobody is thinking is like a joke nobody tells — hard to say what it would even be.

So here’s the big idea: there must be a Mind that has always existed and can never stop existing, that thinks every true thing all at once. That Mind never learned math — it always knew it. And a mind like that, which can’t be missing anything, would also be all-powerful and perfectly good. That’s what people mean by God.

The Augustinian proof says eternal truths and possibilities are like that — ideas in a mind — but because they are necessary and eternal, the mind holding them must be necessary and eternal too, and because they include every possibility, it must know everything and be able to realize any of it.
